7569: Ecological assessment is increasingly required by management regulations to quantify the impact of stressors on estuarine and coastal systems. In this presentation, multivariate analysis of community composition at a national scale is proposed as a standardised and sensitive approach to assessing the effects of two stressors (mud and heavy metal contamination) on estuarine health. Benthic macrofaunal data collected at sites across New Zealand were used in separate canonical analyses of principal coordinates to create Benthic Health Models (BHMs) of the responses of macrofaunal community composition to mud content and metal environmental gradients. In addition to being sensitive to changes in ecosystem health, biotic indices need to be unaffected by different species pools and natural environmental contexts. Accordingly, we tested whether estuarine physical type and regional location affect the index values produced and found that the models were suitable for application in two widespread estuary types and across most regions of New Zealand. We also discuss how this national approach relates to assessments carried out at finer scales (regional and estuary) and demonstrate the application of these models using New Zealand case studies. This approach will enable coastal managers across NZ to track health of their estuaries at relatively low cost.
National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research
7570: Since its discovery in 1976, the Megamouth shark (Megachasma pelagios) has remained an enigmatic species. With only ~100 specimens encountered, most of our understanding of this species is based on studies of deceased specimens. Little is known about the behavior or movement patterns of Megamouths. The species is theorized to comprise a single population with global distribution. Information on population structure and movement patterns is needed to best manage the species. This study investigated Megamouth movement by attaching long term pop-off satellite archival tags to three specimens off Taiwan in the Philippine Sea during the summer 2018. Two tags have transmitted data, 66 days from a 565 centimeter female, and 242 days from a 410 centimeter mature male, with the third tag (437 centimeter female) programmed to transmit in November 2019. We tested for short-term area fidelity, preferable habitat conditions, and the potential of prey based migration. Diurnal vertical migration, light levels, and temperature were studied, as well as water depth, proximity to upwelling, and other oceanographic factors that might contribute to an annual migration. Summer aggregations in Taiwan might make Megamouths vulnerable to fisheries, therefore, an understanding of their movements is vital for focused conservation efforts.
7571: Our environment operates at many different scales and has innumerable intricacies and interdependencies. Two of the environment’s most significant and complex systems are climate and oceans. Both systems intimately effect how we live, make a living as well as the things we value. It is for this reason that climate and oceans are a part of the work programme of many government agencies, and science an integral input into these programmes. Alison will outline the importance of connecting across government to ensure best effects in these significant and complex areas, as well as the value of trusted and clearly communicated science to inform decisions. She will also explain the formation and role of the Forum of Chief Science Advisors (convened by the PMCSA) in working together to ensure a more joined up approach across government, and one that that incorporates a credible science voice.
7572: Since human settlement in New Zealand the coastal marine area has undergone modification of marine ecosystems. The extent of human impact and the effect on individual species is often unknown or inferred from unreliable historical data. New Zealand provides a unique opportunity to investigate the impact of human settlement due to its relatively recent occupation and the availability of well-preserved material from archaeological sites throughout the country. The present study compared fish tissue from ancient and modern time points to investigate changes in trophic level and the proportion of alternative organic matter sources (phytoplankton and kelp) through time. This was accomplished using stable isotope analysis paired with mixing models to translate carbon and nitrogen stable isotope signatures into trophic level and relative contribution of phytoplankton to diet. Three time points, six coastal fish species and two regions were selected for study to determine both regional differences in temporal patterns and the response of different species to human settlement. Results demonstrate changes in trophic position among species and between regions. These data provide an important baseline for understanding the changing role of coastal fish species in coastal ecosystems.

7573: To date, genetic monitoring of Hector’s and Māui dolphins has relied on standard DNA profiling, including mtDNA haplotype, sex and up to 25 microsatellite loci. To enhance the power of genomic monitoring, we are using double-digest, restriction-enzyme associated DNA (ddRAD) sequencing. Libraries for ddRAD sequencing were prepared from biopsy samples collected from Māui dolphins in 2015-2016 and sequenced with an Illumina HiSeq 3000 (150 bp, paired-end). We used strict filtering criteria to identify 1,591 variable loci in the Māui dolphin. With these, we confirmed the identity of n = 48 Māui dolphins previously identified by microsatellite genotyping, and the resulting abundance estimate of N = 62 individuals (95% CL, 55 to 73) using a closed population model. Epigenomic monitoring has included a trial study of age-correlated methylation levels at over 30,000 sites in the Māui and Hector’s genomes using a custom hybridisation array. This will enable the future development of an ‘epigenetic clock’ calibrated with known-age individuals for use as a tool to age dolphins from our DNA register and new biopsy samples. Further analyses are underway to estimate effective population size and to identify parent-offspring pairs with ordinal aging for improved estimation of both census and effective population sizes.

7574: Access to live animals for research is a significant factor limiting seafood research in New Zealand and worldwide. Hatchery-based culture of live animals represents a means to access live, undamaged, rested fish populations, to explore all the life stages of a species, and investigate the diverse characteristics of the animal, which are commonly masked by capture damage and fatigue. To realise these opportunities, Plant and Food Research have been investigating the culture of blue cod or rawaru (Parapercis colias). As a coastal species more common in the cooler temperate South Island, blue cod are highly valued by iwi, the commercial and recreational fishing sectors. This popularity, and the increasing pressures faced by the species, create a need to increase our understanding of this endemic finfish. We present an overview of the successes and challenges associated with the development of blue cod in a hatchery environment, and describe aspects of the project, including the collection of gametes, larval development phases, growth and maturation of the species. Potential opportunities for this species are briefly discussed.

7575: Fisheries scientists and managers have historically relied on various fishery dependent and independent data sources to conduct stock assessments, bycatch estimates, and other ecological analyses. Often, these data sources are generated from logbooks, fisheries observer reports, and other paper formats that might take as much as a year or more to be made available for analysis, in some cases resulting in science and management recommendations that are effectively obsolete upon publication. Recently, several emerging technologies as diverse as satellite remote sensing, electronic data capture devices, and artificial intelligence have vastly improved the ability to effectively and efficiently provide more accurate and timely information for use in fisheries conservation and management. This presentation will identify current and future opportunities for the application of innovative and emerging technologies currently employed and under consideration for use in fisheries monitoring, control, and surveillance that will also provide significant improvements in data available for fisheries conservation and management. These technologies, and the information they will provide, have the potential to greatly improve the capacity of fisheries scientists and managers to understand the ecosystems they are responsible for and, in turn, provide better advice for the conservation and management of fisheries resources and the associated ecosystem.
7576: New Zealand is renowned for its rich record of fossil cetaceans. Several undescribed dolphins with “spear-like” horizontally procumbent teeth and long slender jaws have been found in NZ. No extant cetaceans carry such delicate procumbent teeth; however, many fossil species did. These include New Zealand species Waipatia maerewhenua, Otekaikea marplesi, Otekaikea huata (Platanistoidea) and a Kentriodon sp. Specimen (Delphinoidea), as well as Ediscetus osbornei from South Carolina (USA) (Platanistoidea). Other undescribed species with similar tusks have been found in the South Island Waitaki region and are all considered new species. They are known from partial or whole skulls with 6-10 horizontally procumbent apical teeth in their jaws. Two specimens (OU22397, OU22126) have elongate, attenuate, and dorsoventrally flattened rostra, with tusks embedded in elongate premaxillae. The maxillary teeth are polydont; heterodont in OU22397, and near-homodont in OU22126. The periotic (earbone) has a parabullary sulcus, apparently a derived trait for Platanistoidea – superfamily grouping containing the Ganges river dolphin. The function and phylogenetic significance of tusks in fossil dolphins is still uncertain, although feeding or display are possible functions. Understanding the phylogenetic placement of theses specimens will help elucidate the complex evolutionary history of odontocetes.

7577: New Zealand has the 4th largest exclusive economic zone in the world and is a hotspot for marine diversity. However, many of our marine birds and mammals are at risk, and our coastal waters are degraded due to human and natural stressors. Managing the cumulative effects that arise from these stressors is one of the most urgent and complex problems facing marine managers. It is particularly complicated by fragmented legislative regimes and institutions that struggle to deal with cross-scale interactions, chronic data scarcity, and high levels of uncertainty. Concepts such as the ‘precautionary principle’, ‘best available information’ and ‘adaptive management’, have raised the bar in terms of science information needs for decision-makers. As new offshore activities, such as seabed mining, become more feasible, we need to keep bridging the gap between science, policy and practice. Research to improve our understanding of, and management of, the marine environment is occurring through the initiative of the Sustainable Seas National Science Challenge. The Challenge is in a unique position to bring together different stakeholders into various research projects, which has greatly enhanced the uptake of science information by policy-makers and practitioners.
7578: When considering a consent application for the development of a natural resource, the certainty and resolution of information available to a decision maker is largely contingent on the location and spatial scale of the natural resource. The information void in which a decision maker must operate becomes larger the further offshore a resource exists. This is the primary challenge when making decisions under the EEZ Act. One common question asked by regulators, policy makers, and scientists alike is: How can we make robust decisions in a context with information that is low in resolution, and high in uncertainty? Some of the seemingly obvious solutions that are frequently posited are: more data, extrapolation of observations via models, the precautionary principle, and adaptive management. There are factors that limit the application of these solutions, a primary one being that decision makers must decide on applications at a point in time, and base that decision on the best available information. In this presentation I will briefly cover the information puzzle that is decision making in the EEZ, by providing an overview of some of the common issues encountered by decision makers, while applying both marine scientific, and regulatory lenses to this topic.
7579: As natural resource management shifts from government to community-led place-based approaches, we are discovering the importance of creating deeper dialogue between scientist and community. Community participation in environmental monitoring plays a significant role in addressing this issue, allowing resources to be managed at a local scale; enabling community members to regain their roles as guardians of their environment. This aligns with the acknowledgement that multiple forms of environmental data exist, from the numerical results of scientific methods to the traditional ecological knowledge held by kaitiaki. Acknowledging and communicating these different forms data is crucial in effectively managing our ocean, however successful platforms for achieving this thus far are not so well known. This project investigates the potential of ESRI Story Map ArcGIS, ‘Story Maps’ (https://storymaps.arcgis.com/en) to aid place-based management by Tangata Tiaki (Ministerially Gazetted Customary Fishery Managers) in Customary Protected Areas (Mātaitai and Taiāpure). We describe our practice-based research using the East Otago Taiāpure as a case-study. Here, three Story Maps were created to compile and communicate relevant local environmental data. Transmedia, narrative, and ArcGIS mapping were used to communicate Otago University Aquaculture and Fisheries 301 research. The successes and limitations of the platform have been investigated.
7580: Light, substrate and the surrounding community are three important factors in the formation of subtidal biogenic habitats. All three of these were affected by the 2016 Kaikoura earthquake. Initial subtidal surveys showed that sites with high degrees of uplift had extensive areas of bare rock that had been exposed through the underlying sand and gravel. Sparse propagule supply, high turbidity due to erosion of the coastline and high sediment riverine inputs can hinder recovery of these affected areas. Experimental clearance plots were set up to test the effects of understorey algae (corallines, encrusting reds), substrate type (mudstone, limestone) and supply (with and without surrounding large brown algae) on algal recruitment and growth. Laboratory experiments are also being done to evaluate brown habitat-forming macroalgal germling growth in varying temperature, turbidity and light conditions. How algae respond to these varying conditions is important for gauging the recovery of affected Kaikoura habitats and for understanding how algae respond in high turbidity environments that may be human-induced (such as runoff from forestry, and harbour dredging). Algal responses can also be calibrated to a changing climate change of increased temperatures and turbidity.
7581: New Zealand’s coastal and oceanic waters support a valuable seafood sector, which contributes significantly to the country’s annual economy. Significant risks are posed to this sector from CO2- and climate-induced changes to their surrounding environment. We synthesise NZ-specific information on changes in physical and oceanographic parameters projected for the coming decades (including temperature, pH, salinity, oxygen, circulation, etc). We then evaluate the current state of knowledge of how 32 NZ fisheries species, ranging from shellfisheries to inshore, middle-depths and oceanic species, are influenced by these parameters. This information is then used to determine potential risks to these fisheries in the coming decades. Finally, through detailed case studies of paua, snapper and hoki, respectively, we combine scientific data and fisher expertise in an expert evaluation of these species’ vulnerabilities and, importantly, their adaptation potential. Knowledge of how environmental changes might affect different species is essential so that decisions can be made around the potential implications of change to that fishery and the management options available to mitigate them.
7582: Few southern hemisphere time-series measurements of biogeochemical tracers are available, and this scarcity is a major impediment in understanding the processes underlying the oceanic carbon and nutrient cycles in vast parts of the global oceans. The Munida Time series is located off the south east coast of New Zealand in the South Pacific Ocean. At this site, the marine carbon cycle of subantarctic surface waters has been studied since 1998, providing insight into the seasonal, interannual and long term variability of the carbonate chemistry, including ocean acidification. The area is a sink for atmospheric carbon dioxide, and biological activity is the main driver of the pH and pCO2 seasonal cycles, offsetting the effect of changing seawater temperature. A long term increase in pCO₂ of +1.43 μatm/yr, with corresponding decrease of 0.0015 pH units/yr has been observed over the 21 year long time series.
7583: Non-indigenous species have been more frequently observed in New Zealand waters in recent years, as world travel and trade have expanded and diversified. Their impacts on native species, fisheries and local economies is significant. A better understanding of the dynamics of their growth and spread is paramount to predict future patterns and assess the potential effectiveness of control strategies. Here we show the results from stochastic forward simulations, using parameters inputs from a modelling framework which fits to data on positive species observations, probabilities of establishment and growth rates in different habitats, and vessel traffic between major ports (as a potential additional route of transmission). We are thus able to predict species distribution patterns in the future, forecast the effects of altering habitat and climate on this spread, and assess impacts that different management methods can have on population sizes. We thus show for which species eradication from New Zealand is not feasible.
7584: Given the significant challenges facing shark populations globally, improvements for monitoring changes in shark abundance is critical. Populations of marine species are typically monitored using catch-per-unit-effort or capture-mark-recapture surveys as proxies for abundance. However, these methods may not be reliable for detecting trends or change in population size over time, leading to incorrect or incomplete knowledge about the past and present state of a population, to the detriment of management and conservation objectives. The need for alternate methods has led to the increasing use of genetic and genomic markers to evaluate abundance. Here, we use this type of data and population-genetic models to estimate the abundance of breeders in five age-cohorts from a population of white sharks in eastern Australia and compare our results to previous studies. Our intention is to use these genetically-based metrics for long-term population monitoring. We present our insights into the demography of this population, and provide a useful case study for how these methods may be used to monitor other chondrichthyan populations.
7585: The traditional bone fish hooks (matau) as used by the Maori seem, on first impressions, to be fairly inefficient in shape. After making a few copied examples, experiments were carried out in controlled aquarium situations. The technology and design underpinning the hook’s form were explored. The hooks have since been used out in the ‘real world’ and some of the insights gained from creating and using the facsimile hooks will be shared. The work forms the basis of a hands-on education programme offered to school classes in the Nelson/Marlborough regions.
7586: The aim of this study was to assess population attributes of the intertidal gastropod, Amphibola crenata, for use as a bioindicator species to test the effects of trace metal and nutrient contaminants for NZ estuarine habitats. The study was undertaken at 17 estuarine sites across six different regions including Auckland, Canterbury, Nelson, Southland, Waikato and the West Coast. The population structure (e.g. density and/or length distribution) and condition index (CI) of A. crenata were assessed at mid-tide level. The study showed that A. crenata was highly resistant to low levels of certain trace metal contamination including Cu, Zn, Ni, Cd and Pb. The CI of A. crenata was negatively correlated with sediment trace metals (e.g. As, Cd, Cu, and Zn), reflecting potential utility in CI of A. crenata as a biomarker of metal pollution. The study also identified that sediment nutrients played a significant role in determining the structure of A. crenata populations in intertidal areas, supporting the potential use of this species as an indicator of nutrient pollution. The sensitivity of A. crenata population attributes to environmental contaminants, confirmed that A. crenata could be a good bioindicator species to assess the health condition of NZ estuaries.
7587: Multibeam echosounder technology is rapidly becoming the industry and scientific standard for visualising seafloor characteristics and producing habitat maps. The ability to map the sea floor in such detail has many applications in marine spatial management. Here, we describe our approach to benthic mapping and habitat map production. We discuss how this data is being incorporated into the management of customary protection areas and the potential it has for informing ecosystem based management of marine resources.
7588: Measuring animals and quantifying their growth is crucial to answering many ecological questions. Due to their size, whales are inherently difficult to measure. Kaikōura, New Zealand is one of a few places where sperm whales can be studied close to shore. Study undertaken here since 1990 has revealed a decline in this population, mainly driven by fewer whales visiting in summer. This raises the question of whether size structure has changed seasonally, and whether there has been a concurrent trend over time. This study estimated the sizes of whales (n =35) using inter-pulse intervals (IPI) from acoustic recordings gathered over the past four years of field research. Seasonal differences were found in the size structure of this population, with the largest measured whales visiting in summer and smaller whales visiting in winter (t = 2.65, p <0.05). The accuracy of the IPI method will be investigated using very accurate UAV photogrammetry (mean error = 1%) over the next year. Size estimates will also be gathered using acoustic recordings dating back to 1996 to investigate any changes in size structure of this population, and to investigate growth rates among individuals. These results may help explain the ongoing decline in this population.
7589: Estuary soft sediment ecosystems act as a contaminant filter at the land-ocean interface and perform ecosystem functions, such as denitrification, that can provide resilience to increased nitrogen inputs. The nitrogen that fuels estuarine primary production derives from organic matter breakdown in the sediments (a ‘slow’ pathway that generates ammonium-N) and from pulsed inputs following storms (a ‘fast’ pathway delivering primarily nitrate-N). While coupled nitrification-denitrification in sediments is known to reduce pore water ammonium concentrations, little is known about the capacity of sediments to assimilate nitrate-N in the short term after runoff events. Knowledge of the ecosystem attributes that contribute to nitrogen removal processes and the timescales at which they occur is crucial for estuarine ecosystem management. We conducted investigations at four intertidal sites in Mahurangi Harbour, experimentally enriching the water column in benthic incubation chambers simulating a nutrient laden river plume to test whether intertidal habitats can ‘process’ nitrogen from a runoff event. Initial results indicated differences in sediment oxygen dynamics among sites and treatments, suggesting that local biogeochemical processes can respond quickly to increases in water column nutrient concentrations and that there are differences between habitats.
7590: Seabirds are well recognised as indicators of ocean health and productivity. Studying their demographics (breeding success) and foraging behaviour can offer an insight into at sea conditions in addition to signalling a general decrease in ecosystem health. Such measures, however tend to be ‘slow to report’ and a more rapid signal is needed if we are to react in a meaningful way. To this end, ecophysiology offers a potentially rapid insight into current bird health and thus at sea conditions. Using Hauraki Gulf petrels and shearwaters I will highlight key physiological biomarkers that appear sensitive to change within the marine environment. In particular, blood haemoglobin content appears to track the onset of ENSO cycles and weight loss, indicating an upregulation of oxygen delivery in times of stress. Further, by matching these physiological traits with behavioural modelling (Hidden Markov Models) and endocrine responses (corticosterone) a more integrative snapshot of seabird health can be obtained; potentially leading to more effective management. Depending on the foraging range of the study species, the spatial scale “assayed” and reflected in the bird’s physiology can thus reflect the conditions from ocean basins to local council boundaries, thus providing information for a range of differing management jurisdictions.

7591: Isotopic ecology has been widely used to understand spatial connectivity and trophic interactions in marine systems, but comparisons over long time periods are rare. Preserved specimens from museum collections are valuable sources of tissues, but isotopic signatures are known to be affected by fixatives. The aim of this study was to generate a correction factor for the effects of fixatives on carbon and nitrogen isotopes of bulk fish muscle, also to analyse specific amino acid isotopic signatures. Two specimens of Parapercis colias, Seriolella brama and Oncorhynchus tschawytscha underwent formalin fixation and alcohol preservation and were sampled at different time periods. Using AICc and BIC, the best model explained 80% of the isotopic variation due to fixatives, independent of preservation time. Carbon isotopes of amino acids were not affected by treatments. Although nitrogen was significantly affected by fixatives, relationships among amino acids were constant. We applied our findings to reef fishes from Otago, collected between 1950 and the 2018. While trends showed by herbivorous fish are likely related to recent changes in the nitrogen cycle and CO2 inputs to the system, shifts in trophic level and resource use were linked to changes in habitat and stock size of important commercial species.

7592: Investigating the distribution of apex predators is essential for understanding their habitat requirements and can provide insights into community ecology. In New Zealand, only 11 of at least 113 chondrichthyan species are actively managed, emphasising the need for further research. The data deficient broadnose sevengill shark Notorynchus cepedianus is commonly sighted around coastal New Zealand. This study aimed to increase our understanding of their distribution through quantifying habitat selection in Paterson Inlet, Stewart Island. Baited remote underwater videos and associated environmental variables thought to influence shark distribution, were collected during three sampling trips in 2018 (n = 60 deployments). Individual sevengill sharks were identified through unique markings using photo-ID, and the number of sharks observed per deployment was used as an index of relative abundance. Generalised linear models were used to relate relative abundance of sharks to the suite of environmental predictors in a multi-model inference framework. Based on minimum AICc, the best-fitting model (R-squared = 0.69) showed a positive effect of water temperature and salinity, and a negative effect of ambient light. These results provide important insights into the distribution and ecology of sevengill sharks in New Zealand.
7593: A recent risk assessment for chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras) found some deepwater sharks were at relatively high risk of adverse impacts from fishing. Quantitative data for these species is limited, and some available information has been found to be unreliable. With a better understanding of spatial distributions, our knowledge of the risk to, and the status of these species would be more informed. This information would allow for the evaluation of potential stock boundaries, encourage comparisons of New Zealand population structure with populations elsewhere, and overall, better inform fisheries management. Here, we investigate the suitability of vector-autoregressive spatio-temporal (VAST) models, a predictive modelling approach, to estimate spatio-temporal trends for seven deepwater shark species regularly caught in New Zealand deepwater fisheries: Dalatias licha, Etmopterus granulosus, Centroselachus crepidater, Centrophorus squamosus, Deania calcea, Centroscymnus owstoni, and Scymnodon plunketi. Preliminary results from this analysis will be discussed.

7594: Long term population monitoring of the spiny lobster (Jasus edwardsii) within the Cape Rodney to Okakari Point Marine Reserve has shown a decline to pre-reserve numbers. This could potentially be explained by individuals making offshore migrations across the marine reserve boundary, where fishing is permitted. These offshore movements appear to follow after energetically demanding events, such as mating and moulting. Previous laboratory studies have also indicated that these migrations occur at times when captive lobsters are consuming the most food. Therefore, it is hypothesised that lobsters could be making offshore movements in search of energy-rich offshore feeding grounds. To help understand the reasoning behind these offshore movements a grid of sediment grabs were conducted to describe the distribution of potential lobster prey. In conjunction with these findings, different reef and sand prey species were tested in the laboratory for possible feeding preferences and to describe lobster feeding patterns, handling times and energetics. It is hoped that the findings of this study will help policymakers better understand and accordingly protect these vulnerable and valuable species.
7595: In shallow coastal waters, benthic primary producers fuel food-webs and influence nutrient fluxes across the sediment-water interface. Light is an important variable regulating primary production and varies across multiple temporal scales due to weather, tidal stage and season. Additionally, increased delivery of land-based sediments into coastal waters raises water column turbidity reducing photosynthesis. For intertidal habitats, this reduced light availability during immersion may be offset by low tide production. Despite its importance, there is little published data on how light availability influences benthic primary production and associated nutrient fluxes. To rectify this, we seasonally determined photosynthesis-irradiance (P-I) curves and associated nutrient fluxes in seagrass and microphytobenthic (MPB) dominated habitats using benthic incubation chambers deployed at low and high tide with light levels manipulated using shade cloth. Preliminary results indicate comparable production rates during low and high tide for both seagrass and MPB habitats (~4410 vs 4070 & 1280 vs 1010 µmol O₂ m-2 h-1, respectively) confirming the importance of emmersed production. We also saw evidence of photoinhibition at light levels > 360 µmol photons m-2 s-1. Ultimately, the results of this study will help identify light thresholds of benthic primary producers and demonstrate how altering light regimes influences nutrient processing.
7596: Many scientists may wish to influence the behaviour of Fisheries New Zealand. This talk will outline the scope within which Fisheries New Zealand operates, and its key drivers and limitations. This will include the role of science in decision making, and the key processes and opportunities for external input. Some of these opportunities outlined will include how to best discuss research suggestions with Fisheries New Zealand, where to find out about research we are looking to purchase, the role of scientists within Fisheries NZ and participation in our science review processes. Some of the challenges include navigating our procurement and data provision requirements as well as meeting science working group and management application expectations. It is hoped this talk will lead to better understanding of Fisheries New Zealand’s role and processes as well as encouraging people to become involved in these.
7597: The ocean is important to all indigenous Pacific cultures. For Māori, the ocean is an important element of their identity and social belonging. The relationships they have had and continue to have with their maritime environments is symbiotic and symbolically determining. Māori are intimately connected through their atua (deities) and tūpuna (ancestors), and the coast and sea provide sustenance and protection for their whānau (family). This relationship is often in contention with western views and legislative processes toward the marine space and because Māori hold a different perspective toward the marine environment they are often marginalised in decision-making processes. Epeli Hau’ofa’s “re-imagination of the ocean as a highway that links rather than separates” gave prominence to Pacific and seascape epistemology. Thus, this paper will be particularly concerned with highlighting indigenous knowledge, namely mātauranga (Māori knowledge), focusing on west coast communities with a strong connection to Toheroa (Paphies Venticosa), their interaction with the seascape and the tensions faced when negotiating best practice in regards to managing this taonga (treasured) species.
7598: Shark species tend to have low productivity and are therefore vulnerable to over-fishing. This has resulted in management measures that attempt to reduce shark mortality. The Western and Central Pacific Fishing Commission has implemented no-retention measures for some shark species caught on tuna longlines in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean. As a result, many sharks are now released alive. In this study, popup electronic tags were deployed on 60 shortfin mako sharks and 52 silky sharks released from tuna longlines in New Zealand, Fiji, New Caledonia and Marshall Islands. Survival status was determined for over 100 sharks and mortality rates in the first 60 days post-release were estimated for both species. The tags also collected valuable depth and temperature data with which to describe the species’ use of the water column. Displacements between tag deployment and popup locations provided new information on the scale and direction of mako and silky shark movements. Mako sharks showed clear two-way movement between New Zealand and Fiji/New Caledonia.
7599: New Zealand has committed to establishing a representative network of marine protected areas (MPAs). A network of MPAs that represents more of our marine environment will not only have benefits for marine biodiversity conservation but will also be an important scientific resource. To help address known gaps in habitat representation and inform New Zealand’s future MPA strategy, the Department of Conservation (DOC), Fisheries New Zealand and the Ministry for the Environment have been working collaboratively, under an MPA Science Advisory Group, to strengthen the information base to support future MPA planning. Additionally, new funding via DOC’s Biodiversity 2018 Programme has been allocated to a 4-year work stream to develop an improved approach to establishing MPAs. Recent work has been undertaken in conjunction with NIWA to consider how to classify marine and coastal habitats as a foundation for establishing a representative network. Building on this work is the identification of key ecological areas and optimal areas for biodiversity protection, as well as habitats that are under-represented in the current network. Future work will build on these initiatives to support development of sound marine protection policy and more effective approaches to achieving a New Zealand network of MPAs.
7600: This investigation addresses the biological and ecological attributes for 86 species of elasmobranchs mainly distributed in the southern and entrance regions of the Gulf of California. We built a framework in which all elasmobranch species presently distributed within the study regions were identified and arrange taxonomically from the available literature. We selected 48 species of sharks and 38 species of rays with >10% of their distribution. We collated available life history and ecological parameters and we assigned each species to one of four ecological groups (EGs), which is a flexible and novel way to allocate a large number of species based on habitat use, depth strata (shelf-inshore and shelf-offshore), habitat dependence (freshwater, reef substrate, and sandy substrate), and lifestyle (demersal or pelagic). This framework also included four types of fishing: the artisanal fishery, the semi-industrial fishery, the prawn trawl fishery, and the sardine fishery. Two key biological attributes (maximum age and maximum length of each species), four ecological attributes (trophic level, habitat dependence, depth strata and lifestyle), and nine climate change stressors (sea surface temperature, upwelling, salinity, pH, chlorophyll, dissolved oxygen, sea rise level, sea atmospheric pressure, and green gashouses emissions) that affect sharks and rays in the study area.
The National Fisheries Institute of Mexico
The National Fisheries Institute of Mexico
7601: Based on a growing concern about the impacts of bottom fishing on seabed ecosystems, the United Nations General Assembly has called for the adoption of conservation measures to protect vulnerable marine ecosystems (VMEs). Although spatial management based on open and closed areas present one possible solution, a lack of empirical data on the distribution of VMEs within the high seas means spatial management is often informed by predictions of the spatial distribution of VME indicator taxa. Given the uncertainty associated with these predictions, it is sensible to have a back-stop move-on rule, where fishing vessels are required to move a minimum distance away from locations where VME indicator taxa were encountered. Using bycatch data from 8,850 New Zealand bottom trawls within the South Pacific RFMO Convention Area, we illustrate a data-driven approach for identifying candidate thresholds for triggering move-on responses as a backstop to spatial management measures. We argue that the selection of a final threshold value from a suite of candidate values is a management decision that must balance the sensitivity of the move-on rule with the statistical uncertainty of the modelled distributions of the VME indicator taxa.
Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences
7602: Limited information is available on the fine-scale movements and habitat use of juvenile sharks in very shallow (<1 m) nearshore areas and the factors that drive these behaviours. Active acoustic tracking was used to investigate movements and habitat use of juvenile (683 ± 58 mm TL) blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus) at Orpheus Island, Australia. Six juveniles were tracked for over 65 hours. Juveniles moved in synchrony with tidal cycles, always remaining within very shallow (<1 m) sandy reef flat or reef crest waters during outgoing, low and incoming tides, and using inundated mangrove habitat during higher tides, indicating tidal fluctuations were a major driver of movement and habitat use. Individuals never entered deep water beyond the fringing reef, restricting their movements within water <60 cm deep. In general, linearity and rate of movement were significantly higher during incoming or outgoing tides, whilst these measures were significantly lower during higher tide heights when juveniles were occupying mangrove habitats. The observed behaviour was most likely a predator avoidance strategy, highlighting the importance of mangrove root habitat use by juvenile blacktip reef sharks in coastal nursery areas indicating this may be an important habitat for the young of this species.
7603: Nearly 3 years after the Mw7.8 Kaikōura earthquake, the coastal ecosystem continues to reassemble and reorganize following massive reef upheaval. Ongoing sampling of algal and invertebrate communities shows that some intertidal reefs are showing encouraging signs of recovery, while others are impeded by rapid erosion, shifting sands, and elevated sea surface and air temperatures during summer months. This instability has challenged the recovery of the black-footed abalone (Haliotis iris or pāua), which require highly-specific under-boulder inshore habitats during early life stages. With customary, recreational and commercial fisheries still under emergency closure in the region, pressure is mounting to understand how these populations are recovering. Here we use extensive field surveys to identify specific habitat requirements for juvenile pāua, quantify habitat availability, and document population demographics through time. We also use surveys and experimental constructed boulder reefs to gauge the results of commercial reseeding of hatchery-raised pāua along the coastline. Finally, we discuss the role that customary management areas and marine reserves may play in recovery following natural disaster.
7604: Blue cod has been one of New Zealand’s most valuable domestic fisheries since the 1930s. The majority of commercial catch is taken by cod potting in Southland and in the Chatham Islands. Blue cod is a significant customary fishery for tangata whenua and the most popular recreational finfish species in the South Island. Fisheries New Zealand has engaged with tangata whenua and stakeholders to develop a National Blue Cod Strategy (the strategy). The strategy was developed in response to increasing concerns from tangata whenua and local communities, about localised depletion of blue cod populations in part due to blue cod’s unique biology. The strategy consists of a set of overarching objectives and management goals to drive a more consistent, integrated and proactive management approach for the blue cod fishery. This approach was overall received positively by the public. Public engagement included public drop-in sessions, a specific website and social media messaging, and the use of online surveys.

7605: The Anthropocene has seen a global explosion of ecological disturbances, and maintaining ecosystem functions in the face of escalating rates of species loss has become a priority. Functional diversity is commonly used as a surrogate measure of function, where groups of species with similar functional traits are considered functionally redundant and theoretically buffer against some species loss; but this framework ignores the resistance and recovery capacity of communities that occurs across multiple spatial and temporal scales. We develop a more complete theory of functional resilience to disturbance, linking processes operating across multiple scales of ecological organisation (e.g. individual species tolerances to landscape-scale population connectivity). We explore how different combinations of scale-dependent resilience attributes are linked to functional resilience against disturbances that vary in intensity, spatial-extent, and frequency. 7606: Anecdotal evidence describes the presence of large Macrocystis pyrifera (M.pyrifera) kelp forests along the southern Otago coastline which are now no longer present. There are many different hypotheses why these kelp forests have disappeared but most attribute the loss to an increase in sedimentation in coastal waters due to the downstream effects of gold mining, agriculture, industrialisation, and urbanisation. Anecdotes describe kelp forests that supported Jasus edwarsii, Haliotis iris, Evechinus chloroticus and Odax pullus. Anecdotal evidence such as this, has been shown to be important for inferring historical conditions when there are no long term data sets available. Natural fluctuations and disappearance of entire beds is not uncommon in well studied Californian kelp beds, however, it is important to determine if M.pyrifera forests along the Otago coast disappeared due to anthropogenic implications such as discharged waste waters, agriculture or mining or if it is attributed to natural changes such as El Nino cycles, storms, and rainfall. 7607: Recruitment overfishing, whereby adult spawning stock is so depleted a population can no longer replenish itself, is a serious issue for a number of fisheries worldwide. Maintaining spawner biomass is essential to population sustainability, as simply put, sexually immature individuals cannot reproduce. Novel management schemes are needed to conserve large breeding animals and a combination of harvest slot limits and marine protected areas is one potential solution. Using the iconic, and economically valuable Caribbean spiny lobster, Panulirus argus as our model organism we demonstrate the potential for harvest slot limits and MPAs to rebuild and maintain mature populations throughout the Caribbean. To do so, we used a combination of laboratory experiments that examined reproductive output and clutch quality relative to lobster size, and mathematical modelling of different harvest scenarios. We also investigated the possible effect of increasing the abundance of large lobsters in a population, on other species of value. The results, which demonstrate a positive relationship between size and clutch quality highlight the importance of large lobsters to population sustainability. Furthermore, modelling clearly demonstrated the potential for harvest slot limits and MPAs used in concert, to guard against recruitment overfishing at a range of fishing intensities.

7608: Since October 2015, the NSW Government has been trialling new and emerging technologies for shark detection and deterrence under its 5-year, $16 million Shark Management Strategy. Trials have included shark barriers and nets on the north coast, SMART drumlines, drones, and personal shark deterrents. Preliminary results from the trials indicate that some met their objectives, others need more research, and others were not suitable to the dynamic waters of the NSW coast. The outcomes of the trials will inform the economic and environmental evidence to underpin the future of policy development for shark mitigation in NSW. However, sound government policy also needs the social evidence or licence to meet triple-bottom line aspirations, via analysis of community sentiment towards the trials and outcomes. A variety of survey techniques were used to assess community sentiment towards the new technologies trialled under the Strategy versus traditional shark mitigation measures. Preliminary results indicate an overall preference for non-lethal measures, especially drones; for beachgoers to take personal responsibility for their safety, including by the use of personal shark deterrents; and improving understanding through research.

7609: Resources for biosecurity surveillance are limited, so efficient allocation is important. New Zealand’s national programme of surveillance for non-indigenous marine species (NIMS)—the “Marine High Risk Site Surveillance” (MHRSS)—was established in 2002 and aims to detect incursions of potentially harmful species early in the invasion process. Sites included in the programme were chosen based on assessments of their relative exposure to shipping, and environmental factors that could facilitate establishment of known pests. Although the MHRSS objectives and survey methods have been refined since its inception, the sites have not been re-evaluated to take account of changes in shipping vector and pathway behaviour since 2002. Additionally, survey effort among the sites is not related to the relative likelihood of NIMS entry at each site. We developed a statistical methodology to determine the relative likelihood of NIMS entry at New Zealand ports and to guide allocation of surveillance effort among them. Historical ballast water and biofouling data were used to develop models that were applied to data on vessel arrivals in New Zealand ports over two periods (2000-2005 and 2015-2017) to determine changes in the relative exposure to NIMS from each pathway.

7610: In the context of a rapidly changing climate, long-term monitoring studies are important for understanding how marine top predators respond to environmental variability. The submarine canyon of Kaikōura is a highly productive deep-sea habitat and a foraging ground for sperm whales. The number of whales feeding in the area, however, has declined over the last three decades. This trend could reflect a shift in distribution away from Kaikōura, potentially driven by ecological or oceanographic changes within the whales’ habitat. We investigated the influence of long-term variability in ocean conditions on the abundance of whales at Kaikōura by carrying out a time-series analysis spanning 28 years. Generalized linear models were used to relate abundance estimates to climate indices and remotely-sensed sea surface temperature and chlorophyll. Lower inputs of subantarctic-water to the south of Kaikōura in summer, and warmer sea temperatures in winter, were correlated with fewer whales foraging in the area during the following summer, explaining 59% of inter-annual variability. We suggest the variability in oceanographic conditions results in a lagged effect on local prey availability, potentially contributing to the decline in whale abundance. The results increase our understanding of how a changing ocean affects the distribution of wide-ranging top predators.
7611: Alongside of mangrove and salt-marsh, seagrass has been acknowledged as a productive blue carbon ecosystem, however significantly lost through the world. A first step towards the conservation is mapping and monitoring of extant seagrass meadows. Our literature review has revealed that seagrass mapping is occurring with aerial photos at small scale, but as yet use of satellite data is in its infancy. This research aims to develop a novel approach for seagrass monitoring, using machine learning with data from the Sentinel–2, which has 10 m pixels and is freely available from European Space Agency. We used Tauranga harbour as a validation site to compare ensemble machine learning methods, involving Random Forest (RF), Rotation Forest (RoF), and Canonical Correlation Forest (CCF) with the more traditional Maximum Likelihood technique. Using a group of metrics, including F1, precision, recall, and Kappa index, to evaluate the mapping performance at various scenes in 2018, our result indicated that machine learning techniques outperformed Maximum Likelihood with the best performance of CCF (scores ranging from 0.85 – 0.92). Our study is the first combination of satellite data and state-of-the-art machine learning for seagrass mapping that we are aware of, and promises an effective approach for seagrass monitoring.
7612: Continental shelf seas are dynamic and productive habitats. As such they play a disproportionate role in global carbon, macro- and micro-nutrient cycling. The heterogeneity of these environments across multiple scales is key in supporting diverse faunal communities and moderating benthic biogeochemical cycling. However, there is still uncertainty in how variability affects these processes and under what circumstances shelf sediments act as sources or sinks of carbon and nutrients. We show that heterogeneity is a key structuring force of shelf wide patterns in sediment biogeochemical cycling mediated through habitat modification by a diverse infaunal community. Faunal community activity differs seasonally across habitat types, with consequent changes in sediment-water nutrient transport. Small-scale variations in sediment biogeochemical gradients reveal the importance of specific taxa for creation of microbial hotspots with increased abundance and activity of N-cycling microbes. Our results demonstrate the extent to which invertebrate community structure is both influenced by and creates benthic habitat heterogeneity, mediating biogeochemical cycling in shelf seas at both large and small scales. These observations highlight the dynamic nature of the biodiversity–habitat structure complex and begin to establish generalities of how abiotic and biotic interactions, including feedbacks and linkages, influence macronutrient and carbon exchange in shelf sea ecosystems.

7613: Nelson Bays used to support productive green-lipped mussel, oyster and scallop fisheries, now in severe decline within the last 10 years. A review highlighted sedimentation and bottom contact fishing as potential factors. Because fishing is widespread and trawling and dredging homogenise soft sediment habitats, finding control sites to test for the effects of fishing is difficult. Fortunately, between Golden and Tasman Bays there is a 146 km2 area protected from the use of synthetic nets and shellfish dredges for more than 30 years – the Separation Point Power Fishing Exclusion Zone. This site was used in our Sustainable Seas Innovation Fund project to test the use of sediment coring and paleoecological techniques to investigate historic and contemporary changes to the benthos including changing rates of sedimentation and fishing.
7614: Monitoring of lobster in the Cape Rodney-Okakari Point (CROP) and Tawharanui (TAWH) marine reserves has identified substantial declines over the last 10 years. These declines are believed to be driven by the capture of lobster moving across offshore reserve boundaries. To understand the extent such declines are related to reserve size, lobster populations were surveyed across both reserves and in adjacent non-protected areas using commercial lobster-pots. In effective coastal-reserves, offshore movements will be encompassed within the reserves offshore limits and lobster are expected to increase in abundance and mean sizes towards the reserve’s centre. This was not the case in CROP and TAWH. Spatial analysis revealed little difference in CPUE and mean size between reserve centres and potting stations close to longshore boundaries. Overall, CPUE was 3.5 (±0.3) and 3.4 (±0.4) kg in CROP and TAWH, respectively, and only 0.1 (±0.03) kg in non-protected areas. These results show both reserves provide resistance to the extractive effects of fishing, but suggest the level of resistance is compromised by loss across offshore boundaries. It is suggested that the effectiveness of CROP and TAWH can be improved by extending the reserve boundaries further offshore to encompass the offshore movements of lobster.
7615: The New Zealand scampi, Metanephrops challengeri, is a deep-water crustacean endemic to New Zealand waters. It is a commercially important species that is found at depths of 150 to 800 m. As a high value species, they are a good candidate to investigate the potential for aquaculture. However, due to the depths they live in, there is limited knowledge of their reproductive and larval biology. In this study, aspects of the fecundity and larval development of scampi was examined to assess its aquaculture potential. Female scampi carry a small number of large eggs under their tails for an extended period resulting in well-advanced zoea upon hatching with a truncated pelagic duration. A particular focus of this study has been on rearing the hatchlings through their subsequent development stages to benthic juveniles. The identified zoeal stages of New Zealand scampi will be described, along with a comparison with the known larval development in other members of the Metanephrops genus
7616: A joint-agency initiative lead by Auckland Council with Northland Regional Council and the Ministry for Primary Industries collaboratively worked together to carry out a targeted marine pest survey of the Kaipara and Manukau Harbours. Marine biosecurity experts from NIWA were contracted to conduct the surveys from April to May 2019. The purpose of the surveys was to increase our knowledge of the current marine pest situation, as the last marine biosecurity pest surveys of the harbours were conducted over a decade ago. Traditionally, New Zealand’s east coast receives more attention, including research efforts, than the west coast. So....what lurks in the West? We will be presenting the findings from these two exciting surveys.
7617: In New Zealand (NZ), marine reserve (MR) research has traditionally focused on commercially exploited species. In contrast, the broader ecological effects of MRs on large, mobile predators is less understood. This research thus aimed to investigate the effect of MRs on the distribution of predators, including the broadnose sevengill shark (Notorynchus cepedianus) and meso-predatory elasmobranchs. Stereo-BRUVs (baited remote underwater stereo-video systems) were deployed systematically inside and outside of five MRs in southern NZ between April 2018 and April 2019. A pilot analysis of 54 deployments in Doubtful Sound was conducted, with a suite of binomial general linear models created to assess the effect of protection on spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) while allowing for variations in habitat among deployment locations. Based on AICc values, there was most support for models which included the explanatory variables “depth” and “reserve status”, suggesting a potential MR effect through either direct or indirect processes. This study presents the first attempt to assess the effect of MRs on coastal elasmobranchs in NZ, and the first systematic surveys of the distribution of sevengill sharks in Fiordland.
7618: Marine ecosystems today are under immense pressure from growing populations wanting higher standards of living. From food provision to cultural and recreational opportunities, it all translates into more use and (to date) more waste and pollution. It is rare for any marine area to be affected by a single human activity and local activities are overlain on larger scale activities and changing global processes. In this presentation I discuss the likely changes this requires to the research we do (both fundamental and applied) and the management-knowledge interface. I briefly summarise what we know and don’t know about cumulative effects of multiple stressors, and the relationship between uncertainy and decision making. Finally I discuss some likely pitfalls and ways forward.
7619: In New Zealand, ‘whitebaiting’ describes a recreational and commercial fishery where large shoals of post-larval galaxiids are caught as they migrate from coastal waters into freshwater catchments. The whitebait catch consists mainly of īnanga, with much lower proportions of banded kōkopu, kōaro, giant kōkopu and shortjaw kōkopu. Previous studies, with limited spatial coverage and small sample sizes, have shown regional differences in the size and age of īnanga whitebait, but no studies have compared characteristics of the less common whitebait species across a broad geographic range. Here we present the findings of a large-scale whitebait sampling program over six months in 2015. Over 20,000 whitebait were measured and 1500 fish were aged using otoliths. For all species, whitebait entering southern rivers were larger and older. Whitebait on eastern coasts were smaller and older than those at similar latitudes on western coast. This study is the first to make broad-scale spatial comparisons of the size, age and growth of the five whitebait species. From our findings it is apparent that the whitebait fishery is not comprised of a single meta-population and that spatial differences in oceanic conditions drive local adaptation and variability in early life history traits.
7620: Over 85% of shellfish beds and reefs have been lost globally, along with the many benefits and services that they provide. Restoration efforts have been an important tool in helping to regain some of these lost ecosystem services, but there is a need to define the ecological role shellfish play in the wider ecosystem so that the full benefits from restoration can be realised. Using ecosystem function as a metric of success, we measured fluxes of nutrients and dissolved gases from seven restored Green Lipped mussel beds along a grain size gradient in the Hauraki Gulf, in order to determine the resilience of restored mussel populations to sediment stress. Each restored site was compared to the adjacent subtidal flat. Results indicate that mussel bed restorations were successful at enhancing denitrification, and the effects of mussel bed restoration were most pronounced in sandier habitats. Mussel beds can therefore be important to nutrient dynamics through nutrient regeneration, but the importance of nutrient remineralisation varies in response to organism patchiness, flow conditions and background nutrient concentrations. These data suggest that mussel bed creation can quickly restore ecosystem function, but the effects may be dampened in sites heavily impacted by sediment pollution.
7621: Phytoplankton form the base of marine food webs and the composition of phytoplankton communities can impact the functioning of marine ecosystems. One of the central research questions in marine science is how the interplay of different biotic and abiotic factors influence the community composition and productivity of marine phytoplankton. Understanding these interrelations will allow us to predict how climate change might alter phytoplankton community structures in the future. The impact of environmental stressors on phytoplankton is usually determined in controlled laboratory incubation experiments. However, extrapolation to the natural system can be difficult as these incubation experiments can never truly mimic natural conditions. In particular, food web interactions, mixing speed, and the mixed layer depth are difficult to simulate in laboratory situations. Further, the role of oceanographic features, in addition to environmental conditions, in structuring phytoplankton communities has been increasingly recognised. Here we present data on the phytoplankton distribution across the different water masses of the MUNIDA time series transect over three years. Using a combination of genetic methods, microscopy and Flow Cytometry, we untangle water mass specific patterns and annual changes in phytoplankton distribution across the transect.
7622: Microfibers were added to sediment surface layers to assess the effects of increasing microplastic contamination on various soft sediment ecosystem functions and processes. After an initial biofilm growth period, a common depositing feeding bivalve was added to the chambers to assess the interactions and feedbacks with the microphytobenthos (MPB) and the effects of microplastic contamination. Overall in light conditions the MPB biomass and proportion of diatoms decreased in the sediment with increasing microplastic contamination, despite a significant increase in the dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) availability in the bed. Lowered MPB biomass was associated with the reduction in bivalve activities under light conditions, and less oxygenation of the bed. This is supported by dietary analysis of the bivalves, which suggested energy reserves were being depleted at high microplastic contamination. FA biomarkers were examined for bivalves and sediment in light chambers and displayed opposing trends. A constructed ‘diatom index’ significantly decreased in the sediment, indicating a dominance of other taxa over diatoms, yet it increased in bivalve tissue. This was due to the retention of essential FAs associated with diatoms while others were depleted. Results varied with light climate, highlighting complex interactions between MPB, deposit feeders and microplastics.

7623: While leopard seals (Hydrurga leptonyx; LS) are primarily distributed throughout the Antarctic and Subantarctic regions, recent analysis of sightings indicates that they are prevalent year-round in New Zealand (NZ) waters. As such, LS have recently been reclassified from ‘Vagrant’ to ‘Resident’, by the NZ Government. To drive that reclassification, we examined the NZ LS Database (1200-2019), to identify the regions with a prevalence of LS sightings, and within these, identified predictable occupancy locations. The highest ranked regions (and their internal locations) were; Auckland (Waitemata Harbour, Hauraki Gulf), Otago (Oamaru, Dunedin, Taieri) and Canterbury (Kaikoura, Christchurch, Timaru). Contemporaneous LS sightings in each region were abundant; Auckland (762 records between 2009-2019), Otago (324 records between 2000-2019) and Canterbury (153 records between 2010-2018). Photo-identification indicated that between 2014 and 2018, up to 16 LS occupied any given location, in any given year. Additionally, in sequential years, different individuals were recorded at each location and one LS used multiple regions and locations during a seven-year period. Our findings show that LS exhibit regional and local residency in NZ. To better understand the population ecology, key habitat requirements and threats to this Resident species, Management Authorities and researchers should collaborate in ongoing conservation efforts.

7624: Aotearoa has one of the largest EEZs in the world, spanning from subtropical Rangitāhua (Kermadec Islands) to the subantarctic islands. Our oceans are a global marine biodiversity hot-spot - home to an estimated 65,000 species, many found nowhere else on the planet. Massive biodiversity loss is threatening our way of life, and marine ecosystems are impacted by multiple and cumulative threats. Aotearoa has fully protected less than 0.4% of our oceans which puts us far behind global marine protection targets. However, the potential for an inclusive process that upholds the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi, presents a unique opportunity to be world leaders in ocean protection. We present a pathway for Aotearoa to rapidly step-up action to build ocean health and resilience. We seek to achieve this by supporting an iwi-led approach with a wide range of stakeholders, including our Pacific Ocean partners. Our focus is on building strong relationships to achieve shared goals for ocean health. In this way, we hope to achieve an effectively designed plan for marine protection that conserves biodiversity, underpins sustainable fisheries and enhances resilience to climate change.
7625: Marine mammals can act as sentinels of change in subantarctic environments, reflecting medium and long-term oceanic processes. Southern right whales (SRWs; Eubalaena australis) are ideal for addressing questions about the effects of climate change on Southern Ocean ecosystems; they are capital breeders that cease feeding prior to arriving at their calving grounds where they give birth and support lactation from accumulated fat reserves. Using a UAV-based photogrammetric system we can accurately quantify absolute body size and shape, and thus body condition, with less than 1% error. During an expedition in 2016 to the Auckland Islands, NZ’s primary SRW calving ground, we collected measurements of 75 uniquely identifiable SRWs. Principal component analyses of these data indicate measurements of width, particularly at mid-body (40-60% of total length), are most influential in PC1 (41.8% of variance explained). Measurements of the head and tail flukes relate more closely to PC2 (21.8% variance); all other PCs explained <10% of the variance. These data, annual abundance estimates and photogrammetric data from subsequent expeditions, will be analysed in relation to climate and productivity anomalies in an attempt to identify the key oceanic processes that may affect the recovery of this impacted population.
7626: Unwanted bycatch of undersized and non-target species is a problem in many trawl fisheries. In New Zealand, as well as other parts of the world, there have been efforts to improve trawl selectivity; e.g. increasing the size, and / or changing orientation of the meshes. These changes, and the resulting changes in selective properties of commercial trawl nets are not well documented in New Zealand. This lack of information not only hinders the ability of the fishing industry to demonstrate improvements in sustainability, but may also hinder more widespread uptake, and is not necessarily well accounted for in fisheries management. The aim of this project was to utilize a fisheries modelling and prediction software tool, FISHSELECT, to better understand how changes being made within the fleet will affect catches of undersized fish. We will present selectivity models and predictions from data collected from two trials carried out in inshore Hawkes Bay in 2017 and 2019, and the implications of these results for bycatch mitigation.
7627: Mangroves are productive habitats, offering essential ecological services to inhabitants. A variety of species depend on mangrove habitats, making them one of the biodiversity hotspots in the tropics. However, little attention has been paid to how elasmobranchs use mangrove habitats. Here we review the developing knowledge of the relationship between mangroves and elasmobranchs. A consensus derived from previous studies indicated that mangroves offer elasmobranchs feeding opportunities and refuge from predators, and may serve as nurseries for juveniles of some species. However, a majority of studies merely discussed use of nearshore habitats rather than mangrove systems specifically, resulting in poor understanding of importance of mangroves to elasmobranchs. The trophic role of elasmobranchs within mangrove ecosystems is poorly studied, and whether mangroves play a direct/indirect role in providing food resources to elasmobranchs remains unclear. Use of mangrove-fringed nearshore habitats as nurseries is relatively well examined, although there are species- and regional research biases. Given the status of ongoing mangrove deforestation, knowledge of ecological functions of mangroves for elasmobranchs is urgently required to predict how mangrove loss is affecting their populations. Future research examining mangrove use by elasmobranchs, particularly in the regions that have suffered from significant net loss of mangroves is required.
7628: Bronze whaler sharks (Carcharhinus brachyurus) are a large, mobile, predatory species present throughout the North Island and upper South Island of New Zealand. They occupy a variety of coastal habitats which support a diversity of marine organisms, interacting with complex trophic cascades. Bronze whaler sharks are known to utilise coastal environments during summer months, but little is known about their movements or distribution during the remainder of the year. This research harnesses stable isotope analysis of muscle tissue samples along with satellite tagging to investigate the putative seasonal movements of bronze whaler sharks between coastal and pelagic habitats. Furthermore, their predatory influence as top level predators within associated ecosystems was assessed. Preliminary analysis of stable isotope data indicated a reliance on coastal food sources with no indication of utilisation of pelagic systems. However, this was contradicted by satellite tagging data which demonstrated directed movements into pelagic environments. Such conflicting results highlights the need for further research on this understudied species to further understand the complexities of their habitat use, and the predatory role bronze whaler sharks play in New Zealand’s marine ecosystem.
7629: We are all part of a global community grappling with the implications of climate change for marine management. The work of the Department of Conservation is highly influenced by climate change. We have formed a new marine climate change project team to help focus our thinking to adapt to this challenge and explore opportunities for mitigation. The team is currently focusing work on marine mammals, seabirds, marine protected areas, marine reserve monitoring, coastal adaptation with outcomes for nature, and the opportunity of blue carbon for mitigation. We are also considering how new technologies for mitigation and adaptation can grow in a way that doesn’t compound pressures on our marine ecosystems and special species. Connecting globally for best practice is important. Closer to home, we are keen to ensure we work with Māori, across agencies, and with the science and wider community. We have therefore arranged this special session early in our team formation for dialogue. What is your niche for climate change solutions?
7630: Many near-shore environments, such as kelp forests, exhibit large fluctuations in pH similar to levels projected for the surface of the open ocean by 2100, though they are still vulnerable to ocean acidification (OA). Crustose coralline algae (CCA), important component of these systems, are well adapted to low light environments and may grow in habitats where they are light limited for parts of the year. In such environments CCA might be increasingly affected by decreased light availability and OA. This may be particularly true for early life stages. Using light and seawater pH data from a Southern New Zealand kelp forest, a laboratory experiment was designed. We combined 3 realistic, sub-saturating irradiance levels with OA treatments, to estimate its effects on the recruitment of natural CCA assemblages. Increasing irradiance had a positive effect on recruitment numbers and mean size of recruits, while negative impacts of OA on recruitment numbers (70%reduction) and mean size (51% reduction) were observed, notably at the lowest irradiance level. These results suggest that CCA recruitment is vulnerable to OA, and that these effects will be of importance in kelp forest systems where low light conditions may be further reduced in the future due increased anthropogenic activity.
