7631: The ability to recognise vessels that have potentially risky levels of hull fouling is critical for effective biosecurity clearance of international vessel arrivals. Risk indicators developed by the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) have been informative for identifying high-risk vessels, but quantitative evaluation is needed to assess indicator utility and robustness for determining compliance with biosecurity thresholds. To assess the performance of these indicators, MPI commissioned underwater hull surveys of international commercial vessels arriving to New Zealand. Over a 16-month period, 40 vessels were inspected and assessed for biofouling accumulation. The initial risk indicator thresholds performed poorly at predicting biofouling compliance—this was expected given the values were set to target a subset of non-compliant vessels (i.e., high-risk only). Signal Detection Theory analyses were used to refine the high-risk indicator thresholds, which resulted in a statistically significant improvement in performance (93% correct prediction). These new thresholds and risk indicators are being further tested and trialled by MPI. (Work commissioned for this study was undertaken by Cawthron Institute.)
7632: A recently developed high-resolution model for the top of the south region has been developed to provide water transport and water-column information for the Marlborough Sounds. The physical performance of the model is presented with comparisons of the model outputs to available data. This model represents a intial outcome from a multi-year aquatic animal health programme. As part of the programme’s many objectives, it aims to grow knowledge on the dispersal and connnectivity in this important region. This and other tools will be developed to assist with aquaculture planning to reduce animal health issues between cultured and wild species and to improve management responses to potential future events.
7633: Litter is a major risk to New Zealand’s people, culture, environment and economy, especially when it enters the marine environment. Working in collaboration with the Ministry for the Environment, Statistics New Zealand and the Department of Conservation, Sustainable Coastlines is designing and building a national litter database that portrays an accurate picture of our beach litter problem. To collect the data long-term, we have engaged with communities around Aotearoa, providing them with the training and tools required to take part in the project as ‘Citizen Scientists’, measuring beach litter flux and developing and monitoring the effectiveness of their local solutions to the growing global problem of marine litter. The data collection methodology uses a localised adaptation of the UNEP / IOC marine litter survey guidelines, co-developed by the collaborating government departments, who also worked together in the project design phase. Stats New Zealand has applied the Principles and Protocols for producers of Tier 1 Statistics to the data framework to ensure data is of a standard for use in Environment reporting. Thus, the citizen science-collected data can now be utilised for reporting on litter by government bodies nationwide, as well as for international reporting, including on the Sustainable Development Goals.
7634: Kiribati, an island republic in the Central Pacific, is one of the world’s most economically and physically vulnerable countries, consisting of 33 low lying coral atolls. The capital, Tarawa, and its people are increasingly impacted by sea level rise and the frequency of storm surge inundation. Jacobs was commissioned by New Zealand Government, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade for the Government of Kiribati (GoK), to assess the feasibility of reclaiming 300 Ha of inhabitable land by dredging sand from the lagoon and transforming it to an urban development for up to 35,000 people, resilient to predicted 2200 sea levels. The investigations comprised coastal engineering, urban and landscape design and environmental and social impact assessment. This presentation focusses on the marine environment aspect of the investigations which comprised a number of in-country baseline surveys, use of high-resolution remote sensing for marine habitat classification and consultation with the local community and the GoK. The aim was to understand the sensitivity of the receiving environment, identify risks to the marine environment from dredging, optimise suitable dredging locations whilst minimising as far as possible environmental and social impacts.
7635: In New Zealand, marine reserves have been established nationally to protect important characteristics of our marine space. Supported by Air New Zealand, the Department of Conservation are co-ordinating the Marine Sentinel Sites Programme which seeks to develop and investigate important questions about sentinel marine reserves. Kapiti Island marine reserve is one such site where questions developed by the community lead to an investigation of trophic interactions pre and post marine protection. To do so, a multispecies size-spectrum model has been developed to investigate how protection from fishing impacts fish community composition and size structure over time. Using the 10 most commonly observed fishes from underwater visual census surveys on the rocky reef surrounding Kapiti we demonstrate how the community composition changes between a fished and an unfished state. While larger fishes respond positively to protection, smaller fishes can decline in response to increasing predation pressure. The model will be developed into an app that will allow the community to change the inputs, exploring how different pressures influence community composition and fish size structure around Kapiti. This project will develop an understanding of Kapiti marine reserve trophic interactions, while also building relationships and scientific understandings with those who use it most.
7636: Reports of mortality events of wild shellfish from around New Zealand have increased in incidence since c.2015. Bivalve molluscs, including tuatua Paphies subtriangulata, pipi P. australis, toheroa P. ventricosa, and cockles Austrovenus stutchburyi have been submitted to the Animal Health Laboratory (AHL) for disease investigation. The cause of these mortality events can be difficult to identify because they are often multifactorial. The frequent observation of intracellular bacteria – Rickettsia-like organisms (RLOs) – within the gills and intestines suggest these bacteria are important to shellfish health. A paucity of data on RLOs have prevented species identification, precluding any investigation into the role of these bacteria in shellfish mortality events. Tissue samples collected during previous years’ mortality events archived at AHL and samples of contemporary shellfish mortality events were used to generate 16S rRNA gene nucleotide sequences to identify these bacteria. For all RLO-positive animals, nucleotide sequences returned >95% homology to Endozoicomonas species and their presence was confirmed by in-situ hybridization. These new molecular data enable more sensitive and specific screening of these bacteria in New Zealand shellfish to better understand the host-pathogen-environment relationship and what factors contribute to the development of disease.
7637: Gillnets are highly size selective fishing gears and used in commercial fisheries worldwide. Knowledge on size selectivity is important for fisheries management for optimizing catch of target species. Few gillnet size selectivity studies have been conducted on sharks, and even less on rays. Data was collected through an observer survey from the Queensland East Coast Inshore Finfish Fishery operating within the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage area. Size selectivity of nine shark and ray species were estimated using a maximum likelihood models to fit a gamma distributions for different mesh sizes. Preliminary results reveal similarities in θ1 (mode of selectivity curve) between similar species within the same Genus (Charcharhinus and Rhizoprionodon). Values of θ2 (skewness of selectivity curve) ranged from 27 359.34 to 178 384.72, and species with morphologies that increased likelihood of capture (e.g. Anoxypristis and Sphyrna) having higher values. Information from this study can aid fisheries managers and scientists in selecting appropriate gillnet mesh sizes for optimizing sustainable catch of target species, improve information on population dynamics, or reduce shark bycatch.
7638: Spatial management of threats to highly endangered marine species may require a measure of precaution where there is uncertainty in knowledge of species distribution, and when distributions are changing due to global warming. A precautionary approach to establishing protection zones or Marine Protected Areas often include a “buffer”. However there are few examples of robust methods for spatially delineating buffer zones. This talk will explore methods to develop precautionary buffer zones based on the latest habitat modelling developed for Māui and Hectors dolphins in New Zealand. We will illustrate how a buffer can be spatially defined using data about temporal variability in important habitat variables; the quantity and character of uncertainty in habitat modelling; and information outside the modelling, such as verified public sightings. An effective approach to define spatial buffer zones around protected areas for highly endangered animals should make smart use of limited data, and combine data from different sources. There is scope to improve modelling here in New Zealand and help answer questions of international relevance about the relationship between spatial uncertainty in species distribution, and precautionary management in an era of climate change.
7639: Broadnose sevengill sharks are a marine predator found around coastal New Zealand. Data on this species is severely lacking and anthropogenic impacts are unquantified. This hinders sound conservation and management practices. To partially address this, we investigated the population demographics of sevengill sharks in Paterson Inlet, Stewart Island between winter 2016 to spring 2017. A baited remote stereo-video system (BRUV) was deployed to capture underwater video of sharks for photo-ID capture-recapture (using Huggins Robust Design) and photogrammetry analysis. A seasonal trend in abundance of the population was found with more individuals present in the area in spring to summer. The sex ratio was heavily biased, with females comprising 82% of the total identified population. Total lengths ranged from 149 to 276 cm with no apparent difference in size classes of sharks between seasons. This represents the first study of population demographics of sevengill sharks in New Zealand. The techniques employed during this study have been further applied to a citizen science programme focusing on the shark species of coastal Dunedin. This programme targets school groups for educational purposes, as well as allowing the wider Dunedin community a platform with which to inform and be informed about sharks in their backyard.
7640: Patterns of genetic diversity provide a window into the past and present demography of a focal species, and can inform their conservation management. Despite the potential for genetic diversity information from a whole assemblage of species to provide insight regarding the origin, maintenance, and future of biodiversity, there have been few synthetic analyses of genetic diversity patterns in the marine environment. Many researchers independently collect genetic data for marine organisms, but combining these data has been previously impeded by data accessibility and interoperability of database infrastructures. The Diversity of the Indo-Pacific Network (DIPnet) has formed the Genomic Observatory Metadatabase (GeOMe) to provide a centralised repository for genetic data. GeOMe is now the most extensive database of georeferenced DNA sequences comprising over 36,000 individuals and 230 species. I will present the first multispecies, synthetic analyses regarding genetic diversity patterns for Indo-Pacific marine organisms, conducted by DIPnet and based on GeOMe data. I will then discuss extension of the network into New Zealand. The Ira Moana - Genes of the Sea - Project invites the participation of all marine researchers who produce genetic and genomic data, or have an interest in using genetic data to help us manage our marine environment.
7641: New Zealand arrow squid, Nototodarus sloanii (Gray, 1849) and N. gouldi (McCoy, 1888), play an important role in the diets of humans and other predators. This study compares trace element concentrations (As, Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Hg, Ni, Mn, Pb, V, and Zn) in the two species from different locations within New Zealand’s Exclusive Economic Zone. Muscular mantle tissue, which is consumed by humans, and digestive gland tissue (the primary organ for metal accumulation), have been compared from male and female specimens from seven sampling locations (Auckland Islands, Chatham Rise, Dunedin, Kermadec Islands, Golden Bay, New Plymouth and the West Coast of the South Island). In particular, Cd and Hg concentrations were higher in the tissue samples from around New Plymouth. The dietary consequences for humans have been assessed using simulated in-vitro digestion. Arrow squid can be considered an important vector of trace metal transfer to top predators with regional specific differences.
7642: Climate change effects on the physics and chemistry of the ocean are recognised as a happening thing across government in New Zealand as well as the seafood sector. The data provided by the science community shows that trends in New Zealand waters parallel observations across the globe both in terms of trend and in the occurrence of extreme events. Fisheries New Zealand has four projects underway to investigate the risks and opportunities to the seafood sector, detecting fish population shifts, exploring the impact of change on stock assessment model assumptions about the productivity of fish stocks, and, evidence for regime shifts in the Subantarctic. Using the science to inform decision-makers about adaptation or mitigation measures in fisheries however seems to be a slow process across the globe. We are in new territory. Predictive studies and projections change according to climate models selected and the management system is not well suited for large environmental changes. This talk will provide an overview of where Fisheries New Zealand is up to in terms of providing science advice to managers about climate change and ocean acidification effects on fisheries and summarise the next steps on information needs.
7643: Phosphorus (P) acts as a limiting factor for marine microbial productivity. When inorganic phosphate (Pi) is scarce, microbes recycle dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP) to satisfy P-requirements. Phosphonates, characterized by the stable C-P bond, comprise ~25% of DOP. In this study, we extensively surveyed the genomic and metagenomic distribution of genes directing production and degradation of two relevant marine phosphonates: 2-AEPn and methylphosphonate (MPn). We curated publicly available protein sequences to create enzyme databases used for phylogenetic analysis and screening metagenomes. Metagenomic analysis was performed on the publicly available Tara Oceans dataset and the Munida Microbial Observatory Time Series (MOTS), a four-year transect spanning subtropical and sub-Antarctic waters off New Zealand. Genes for phosphonate production were found in 20% of the surface community, increasing to over 50% of the deep ocean community. Pathways for 2-AEPn degradation were 20-fold to 50-fold more common than MPn degradation. Several classes, including Alphaproteobacteria, Deltaproteobacteria, and Synechococcales, contain genes for 2-AEPn scavenging, while MPn degradation was primarily limited to Alphaproteobacteria. In surface waters, presence of production and degradation pathways increased by up to 2.5-fold during winter months. Our results provide spatiotemporal context to the global marine phosphorus economy, suggesting a dichotomy in phosphonate scavenging strategies.
7644: Benthic primary production is an important ecosystem function and an integrative marine environmental indicator that can be assessed by analysing benthic oxygen exchange (i.e., dissolved oxygen fluxes). Aquatic eddy covariance is a technique for measuring oxygen fluxes based on the covariance between vertical current velocities and dissolved oxygen concentrations in small parcels of seawater (eddies) that flow past sensors positioned near the seafloor. The method requires accurate, high-frequency, coupled measurements of currents and oxygen. It has the advantage of being non-invasive (nothing is inserted or removed from the habitat of interest), and is applicable in a variety of common coastal habitat types including unvegetated soft-sediments, rocky reef algal turfs, rhodolith beds, seagrass, etc. Preliminary eddy covariance data from a muddy subtidal habitat in Mahurangi Harbour (four instrument arrays deployed for 5 days and nights) and further applications and limitations of the method will be discussed.
7645: Spinal anomalies are a source of downgrading in finfish aquaculture with a typically multifactorial aetiology. In farmed New Zealand king salmon, spinal curvatures in the form of lordosis (L), kyphosis (K) and scoliosis (S) are known to develop late in seawater production. However, much about their pathology is unclear, leading to difficulties in identifying the factors responsible. We radiographically documented the development of spinal curvatures in two cohorts of commercially-farmed New Zealand king salmon throughout seawater production. Curvature onset occurred 7-10 months post-seawater transfer. Kyphosis and lordosis occurred with a similar prevalence and frequently co-existed. Scoliosis was generally only observed when both lordosis and kyphosis were also present, and most affected fish at harvest possessed all three phenotypes. Lordosis primarily developed in the cranial and trunco-caudal spinal regions, and kyphosis in the trunco-cranial and caudal regions. Scoliosis was predominantly associated with the truncal spine. An “LKS complex”-like phenotype – serial repetition of lordosis, kyphosis and scoliosis along the cranio-caudal axis – was frequently observed at harvest. Onset of concurrent vertebral body anomalies, namely compressions and dislocations, generally proceeded curvature development. Spinal curvatures in farmed New Zealand king salmon appear to constitute a rapidly-progressing, late-onset “LKS complex”-like condition with a likely neuromuscular origin.
7646: On 15 May 2018, New Zealand became the first country in the world to enforce national regulations to manage the biosecurity risks associated with vessel biofouling. The Craft Risk Management Standard for Biofouling (CRMS) requires vessels to provide evidence of biofouling management to the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) prior to arrival in New Zealand, giving MPI unique insight into vessel maintenance practices within the maritime industry. Throughout the first year of enforcement, the rate of compliance with the CRMS has steadily increased, indicating a shift in behaviour within the industry driven by the regulation. During this period, MPI engaged with various sectors of the maritime industry, led outreach and training campaigns, and tested new detection technologies in order to ensure a high rate of compliance. This presentation summarises the insights gained during the first year of enforcement of the CRMS, and directions moving forward.
7647: Many sharks use inshore coastal waters during part of their life cycle, where they are susceptible to a range of human produced environmental changes. Rig sharks (Mustelus lenticulatus) migrate to sheltered harbours and estuaries around New Zealand to give birth and to mate. To understand how rig sharks use these coastal waters and therefore how susceptible they are to environmental change, 62 adult rig sharks were tracked within Pauatahanui Inlet, a spawning and nursery area, using GPS tags. The season length was determined, the areas rig sharks used and didn’t use were identified, the behaviour of the sharks in each location was determined using Hidden Markov Modelling, and the environmental variables likely to affect rig movement were analysed. Rig sharks avoid intertidal areas, show five different behavioural traits, and their movements were most likely influenced by sedimentation, water depth, prey density and distribution, and water salinity.
7648: The New Zealand scampi (Metanephrops challengeri) is a commercially important crustacean that is caught around New Zealand using bottom trawls. To reduce the environmental impact of these trawling methods, research efforts have been aimed at developing new potting technology. Critical to the effectiveness of these pots is the attraction of scampi to the bait, however, very little is known about the chemosensory and foraging behaviour of New Zealand scampi. To understand this behaviour, a series of laboratory assays were used to investigate scampi foraging behaviour. We found that scampi foraging behaviour varies in response to different baits, that scampi are more efficient foragers in turbulent conditions, and that New Zealand pilchard (Sardinops neopilchardus) was the most attractive of the baits we trialled. The combined results of these experiments suggest that scampi are opportunistic scavengers that venture out of their burrows during periods of higher tidal flow to search for food. Consequently, pots should be fished during periods of high tidal flow, using pilchards or other oily fish as bait.
7649: Nutrient pollution is a major problem for marine ecosystems in New Zealand and throughout the world. However, its effects on microphytobenthos (MPB), an important primary producing component, remain unclear. To study the responses of MPB to nutrient enrichment, we executed a nutrient diffusing substrata (NDS) experiment at the Avon-Heathcote estuary, Christchurch. Three NDS containing trays were deployed at the sites with high, medium and low amounts of nutrients in the water column. After 25 days of colonization by surrounding MPB, all NDS were brought back to the laboratory for the estimation of MPB biomass and primary productivity. We hypothesized that both N and P enrichment will have positive effects on MPB biomass and primary productivity rates at the sites with low and medium amounts of water column nutrients. Our results showed that the MPB have increased their biomass on all experimental sites, but only in response to N addition. However, the increases in biomass did not translate into higher primary productivity. This can be explained by a shift in MPB community composition towards the dominance of the species with higher turnover and lower primary production capability.

7650: The penetration of light to the sea floor within coastal ecosystems provides the basis for productivity through benthic primary production. This productivity fuels adjacent food webs and influences organic matter processing, carbon cycling and the transformation of nutrients. Globally, many intertidal ecosystems are either too turbid during inundation to allow benthic photosynthesis to occur or are starting to shift towards this altered ecosystem state. To compensate for this inhibition of photosynthesis, high productivity can occur during emersion, however, modifications to other functions such as nutrient processing are not so readily substituted. We deployed PAR sensors at 22 sites within 14 estuaries spanning a 10° latitudinal gradient across New Zealand to assess variability in light availability at the sediment surface of intertidal sandflats. We supplement this time series with in situ oxygen flux data during inundation and carbon dioxide flux data during emersion, before estimating whether productivity during emersion could compensate for this reduction. Our results highlight the importance of emerged productivity and identify intertidal regions as crucial habitats in highly turbid estuaries. The predicted global decline in the extent of intertidal habitats owing to sea level rise may therefore increase the vulnerability of these ecosystems as productive regions are lost.
7651: Understanding how species coexist, and thus how diversity is maintained in biological communities, is a major challenge of community ecology. Key insights into potential coexistence mechanisms have focused on the strength of interactions among neighbouring individuals of co-occurring species. Yet the majority of theories and empirical tests of these take place in annual-plant communities and in relatively low diversity situations. In an attempt to broaden our insights into coexistence mechanisms, we measured species interactions in diverse, marine fouling communities. Marine fouling communities consist of sessile invertebrate taxa, which inhabit hard substrates such as rocky reefs and man-made structures of marinas. We examined experimentally-manipulated marine fouling communities and quantified changes in percent cover of abundant taxa over four months. We then used these changes to infer the effects of co-occurring species on 10 focal individual species finding both competitive and facilitative interactions depending on the focal species. These interaction estimates then allow us to predict the coexistence of some marine fouling communities. While variable, disentangling the effects of these interactions represents in turn coexistence represents an important step in understanding the maintenance of diversity in benthic marine ecosystems.
7652: The Avon-Heathcote Estuary/Ihutai is one of the best studied estuaries in New Zealand and has a long history of documented anthropogenic change. Earthquake activity, centred in Te Ihutai in 2010/2011 involved severe shaking , uplift and sinking together with large inputs of liquefaction sediment. Damaged sewerage systems also resulted in large inputs of untreated sewage. Built in 2010, it had been hoped that the ocean pipeline would improve water quality and intertidal communities in Te Ihutai. This presentation summarises the large and small scale changes which have occurred in Te Ihutai post earthquake and reports on the rates of recovery of mudflat communities. As expected, surface dwelling species rapidly invaded bare mudflat surfaces and there was some juvenile recruitment. Some long lived bivalve species such as Tuaki survived the disturbances and continued to grow and reproduce. Although seagrass and saltmarsh species had much slower recovery, there have been range extensions and recruitment into new areas. With more area now available for wetland expansion, the hope is that communities in Te Ihutai will improve further over the next ten years.
7653: The enigmatic Fiordland penguins or tawaki breed along a stretch of only 500 km of coastline in New Zealand’s rugged and inaccessible southwest. Despite their limited distribution, tawaki occupy remarkably diverse marine habitats. In 2014, the Tawaki Project set out to study the penguins’ ecology across their breeding range. We examined the penguins’ foraging behavior at three sites representative of the species’ distinct habitats. Over the course of five years, we witnessed the impact of El Niño on foraging ranges and breeding success, documented the effects of an incursion of stoats and followed the penguins’ extreme long-distance movements outside of the breeding period which at a first glance defied all logic. Data we collected paint an intriguing picture of a crested penguin species that apparently lives well outside its genus’ comfort zone (subtropical instead of subantarctic waters). Tawaki have established themselves in a set of different ecological niches, which may enhance the species resilience to environmental perturbations. Here, we present a summary of the first five years of the project and illustrate how tawaki’s versatile marine life-style enables them to cope with environmental change.

7654: Penguins have dense bones predisposing them towards fossilisation. This, alongside habitat and burial conditions, explains the excellent fossil penguin record in New Zealand. Our endemic genus Platydyptes is one of the world’s few described genera from the later part of Oligocene age (~23-25 million years ago), when New Zealand was an archipelago surrounded by shallow seas. Platydyptes is the most crownward of the stem or basal penguins - a precursor for the modern radiation. Since the early studies by Marples in 1952 and Simpson in 1971, informative new specimens have been recovered including partial skeletons. Platydyptes has three named species, differentiated by size of the humerus: P. novaezealandiae (humerus length = 104mm), P. amiesi (hl = 117mm), and P. marplesi (hl= 93mm). A new semi-articulated partial skeleton suggests a fourth species, with a humerus (hl=119mm) distinctly broader than the other three. Current research involves reconstructing the body plan for each species, to elucidate ecological partitioning of the 3-4 coeval and apparently sympatric species. For instance skeletal reconstruction of P. novaezealandiae gives an estimated bill to vent length of 950mm, comparable to living species of Aptenodytes. This study will reveal insight to the structure, systematics and lifestyle of New Zealand’s Platydyptes.
7655: Taxonomy is fundamental for providing a framework to understand the natural world, and is necessary for global conservation. Comprehensive descriptions that include suitable photographs are essential for proper identification of sponge species, especially within groups such as Dysidea, where there are no spicules to differentiate taxa. Historically, Dysidea specimens collected from around New Zealand have been few in number, and were usually degraded, having limited taxonomic value. Here, we describe two new species of Dysidea collected from Tauranga Harbour, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand, differentiating them from all other Dysidea species described. Dysidea tauranga sp. nov. and Dysidea elvieae sp. nov. Furthermore, this novel work confirms a total of five valid species of Dysidea that are all endemic to New Zealand with: Dysidea cristagalli Bergquist, 1961a, discovered from Noises Island, Ragitoto; Dysidea navicularis Lendenfeld, 1888, discovered from Port Lyttelton; Dysidea spiculivora Dendy, 1924, discovered from Three Kings Islands and Cape Maria Van Diemen; The species descriptions herein are significant in at least two major respects. Firstly, they confirm that New Zealand supports the second highest diversity of valid Dysidea species worldwide. Secondly, these descriptions significantly strengthen the basis for future taxonomic work on New Zealand Dysidea species.
7656: Development of high input farming of salmon creates challenges and opportunities in the context of ecosystem-based management. Active aquaculture produces organic wastes in the form of waste feed and fecal matter which become available as an organic matter source for wild communities. Salmon farming, along with other human activities also has the potential to act as a source of organic compounds, with tendencies to bioaccumulate and biomagnify in wild food webs. This is a topic of interest both in terms of the implications for human health and for the marine ecosystems within the farms’ ‘zone of impact’. Here we have used environmental chemistry to model the fate of organic waste from aquaculture into key members of the surrounding reef communities and to measure levels of organic compounds of interest in these species and in salmon feed. Our findings indicate that bulk and compound specific stable isotope analyses are required to track uptake of organic waste by reef communities. We also suggest that elevated levels of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) detected in species around some farms warrant further investigation into potential sources of these POPs. Results from this study have implications for understanding how marine communities may respond to further development and expansion of aquaculture and how negative impacts may be mitigated.
7657: We assessed the extent to which phenotypic plasticity and genetic adaptation influence survival rates of the endangered Yellow-eyed penguin (YEP; Megadyptes antipodes). Using a dataset of 2123 birds that were individually marked since the early 1980s (Otago Peninsula), we developed a Bayesian capture-recapture model that was capable of decomposing phenotypic variance of survival into variance due to genetic and environmental effects. Our analysis revealed a positive genetic trend of fledgling survival, which increased annually by 3% at the genotypic level. As such, the current population should be in a better state than seen historically. However, after disaggregating the data into genetic lines with low and high fledgling survival (relative to the population average), we found that both groups were negatively affected by increasing sea surface temperature. For example, in cooler than usual years, the chance to survive was 53% and 98% for genetic lines with low and high fledgling survival, respectively. These survival rates dropped to 0.4% and 2% respectively during the hottest years. Thus, our results indicate that a positive change in fledgling survival due to selection might be obscured by environmental changes and that the decline of YEPs is linked to low adaptive potential to deteriorating environmental conditions.

7658: There is a paucity of information related to the Southern Hemisphere subspecies of the long-finned pilot whale, Globicephala melas edwardii with most information in New Zealand (NZ) waters from stranded animals. The species is found year-round in NZ waters but more frequently observed in the warmer-water months. Here we focus on the demographics and social associations of free-ranging long-finned pilot whales that frequent northern NZ waters. Between December 2003 and September 2018, we collected photographs of 64 groups of pilot whales with an average group size of 52 (S.E. = 5). A total of 43,832 images were quality controlled and given an image and distinctiveness score and integrated into a photo-identification catalogue. Using the social network analysis program SOCPROG, we will determine individual association patterns over the 15-year study period. This information will be compared to the results of similar studies in the Northern Hemisphere, to better understand whether the two subspecies of long-finned pilot whale have equally complex social organizations. Gaining an insight into their social structure provides an opportunity to understand the biology of the species and may aid in improving future strandings-management strategies.
Institute of Marine Science, University of Auckland

7659: Zooplankton such as krill, copepods, and salps are key to Southern Ocean ecosystem functioning. Within food webs, these organisms drive the quality and quantity of energy transferred from primary producers to higher trophic levels. In terms of element cycling, zooplankton body mass and fecal pellets can contribute significantly to carbon export from surface waters to depth, especially during bloom events. However, our limited knowledge of when and where different zooplankton populations occur in New Zealand waters restricts our ability to link the physical environment to the impact of their ecological roles, which is crucial for predicting and recognizing ecosystem shifts induced by future environmental changes. The twenty-year history of physical data from the Munida Time-Series provides a great scaffold upon which to build our understanding of biological components such as microbial diversity, and now for the first time, zooplankton. Every two months from November 2017 to September 2018 we collected surface zooplankton (<200m) at each of the eight Munida stations and analysed samples for species abundance and diversity. Here we present the first look at spatial and temporal zooplankton distribution along the Munida Transect and discuss implications of this new data set in both local and global contexts.

7660: Shellfish are globally important to marine systems and the socioeconomics of coastal communities, and in New Zealand are taonga to iwi. Many wild shellfish populations are under increasing threats from multiple stressors. Mortality events from disease have increased, and some populations have declined markedly. Co-infections with multiple pathogens are implicated in some disease outbreaks, but their interactions are not well understood. Climatic and environmental stressors can also contribute to increased disease in shellfish. Pathogens may play key roles in shellfish dynamics and may trigger regime shifts in population productivity. Since the 1985 Bonamia exitiosa epizootic in Foveaux Strait oysters (Ostrea chilensis), there has been a regime shift in fishery productivity. Cyclic mortality from B. exitiosa has limited the persistence of high density, localised populations. The effects of disease mortality on the stock are described along with a preliminary investigation of the potential contributions of factors other than stock size to low recruitment. Infections and high oyster densities are implicated in recruitment failure; however, a 3-way interaction between oyster density, disease, and climate are more likely to drive variation in recruitment. Pathobiomes may be important determinants of shellfish recruitment and population dynamics.
NIWA; Victoria University of Wellington; Victoria University Coastal Ecology Lab (VCEL)
7661: The unprecedented availability of species data is contributing to a paradigm shift in biodiversity research, where a more data-centred approach is being used. In conjunction with increasing awareness and concern over the continuing loss of global biodiversity, interest in these global open-access data sources has grown. In this study, we used data from online databases and literature to show that marine parasitic discovery rates are far below that of non-parasitic marine species. These results show that species discovery rates between marine non-parasitic species and parasites is widening. We examined if this may be a product of taxonomic productivity, yet this is at its highest rate ever recorded. To gain more insight, we analysed chondrichthyans and their parasites and found that just over a third of all known chondrichthyan species have had their parasite communities surveyed. Of these, there is an average 99-year lag from when the host is described to when its parasite is described. However, as more hosts are surveyed, biologists are finding species that have previously been described. These findings suggest that marine parasites are less host specific than literature is suggesting and propose that these organisms can inhabit which ever suitable host they encounter during their life-cycle.

7662: Depending upon location, 2, 3, or 4 species of Peltorhampus may be collected simultaneously. Sympatric distributions present opportunities for comparative study of life histories and ecologies of these interesting flatfishes. Data extracted from 1868 museum specimens and from literature sources indicate that these flatfishes are found primarily in shallow waters (0.5-50 m) off both islands. Juveniles of two species occur at similar depths occupied by adults; data are too limited to determine juvenile habitats for the other species. Except for P. novaezeelandiae (ca. 550 mm SL), the remaining three species, P. tenuis, P. latus, and Peltorhamphus n. sp., are relatively small-sized, reaching to about ≤160 mm SL. Males and females reach similar maximum sizes in three of four species; only P. latus is sexually dimorphic with females attaining a greater (144 mm SL) size compared with that (126 mm SL) of males. Although no differences were found in the present study, some literature indicates that female P. novaezeelandiae reach larger sizes than do males. Size and maturity data for each species reveal differences among species in female size at maturity. Information on depths of occurrence, sizes at depth, and habitat utilization were assessed and compared among the four species.

7663: The shells of large benthic foraminifers (LBF) are key contributors to the development and maintenance of coastal landforms in the Pacific. The current study attempts to explain the biology of LBF in terms of their locomotion, fecundity, and survival from different sites of Viti Levu, Fiji. Accordingly, two major groups of benthic foraminifera, namely Marginopora vertebralis Quoy and Gaimard, 1830, and Amphistegina lobifera Larsen 1976, were examined under laboratory conditions. The two species of foraminifera were cultured for 12 months while maintaining the natural reef-flat environmental conditions. Physicochemical parameters, such as salinity, alkalinity, pH, and temperature varied by <5% throughout the culture experiment. Results indicate that the fecundity of the M. vertebralis varied directly with parent size, with a mean of 2.7 x 10² offspring produced per adult while A. lobifera produced a mean of 4.8 x 10² offspring per adult. The minimum size of reproduction of M. vertebralis was 15 mm, and A. lobifera reproduced at 1.4 mm. The results from the culture experiment indicate that our culturing conditions can successfully reproduce environments similar to the natural habitat

7664: Macrofauna play a key role in the structure and functioning of coastal soft-sediment systems by regulation of key processes such as nutrient exchange, sediment stability and organic matter remineralisation. Changes in wave energy can influence sediment stability, altering particle size, cohesion and water content. Sediment resuspension is also influenced by benthic macrofauna, as organisms alter the intrinsic sediment properties through their activities and behaviours. We examine the effects of a key tellinid bivalve, Macomona liliana, on sediment stability along a gradient of wave exposure in Tauranga Harbour. Three mid-intertidal sites were selected to span a range of tidal currents and wind-wave exposures in order to determine the importance of bioturbation in controlling sediment stability, relative to that of physical resuspension. At each site, plots were manipulated to create density gradients (0 – 470 adults m-2) and were left up to 9 weeks before measures of sediment stability were undertaken using ex-situ annular flumes. Sediment samples were also collected to elucidate variability. Manipulations and measurements were also repeated seasonally. Mass of sediment eroded (ME; gm-2), mean erosion rates (ER; mg m-2 s-1) and critical erosion velocities (Ucrit; m s-1) will be discussed in association with their biotic or abiotic predictors
7665: Crustaceans are amongst some of the most successful marine invaders. As invasive species are the second biggest driver of global biodiversity loss, it is important to understand their impacts for conservation measures. The Japanese mantis shrimp (Oratosquilla oratoria) is a large stomatopod crustacean that was first officially reported in the Kaipara Harbour in 2010. To estimate its impacts, fishermen were interviewed to establish its pattern of expansion and population density. Potential habitat was estimated through sediment preference tests and physical preferences from its native range, and ecological impacts were estimated through diet preference tests and fishermen observations. Fishermen reports revealed a range expansion on the west coast and to the east coast, as well as a significant population decline in 2018, with rig and snapper reported as predators. Sediment tests indicated a preference for 'sandy mud', and its distribution is not likely to be limited by sea surface temperature. Polychaete worms and snapping shrimps had highest preference in diet tests, but it can also prey on harder-shelled species. Though the population crash may lessen its impact, a cautionary approach should be used in light of its significant expansion and variable diet.
National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research
7666: How robust are fisheries assessments and management to effects of climate variability and change? Increasing temperatures under climate change are thought to affect individual physiology of fish and other ectotherms through increases in metabolic demands, leading to changes in species performance with concomitant effects on species ecology. Here, we develop a general size and trait-based model of energy and oxygen budgets to determine the relative influence of metabolic rates, oxygen limitation, and environmental conditions on ectotherm performance. We then embed this eco-physiological model in a trait-based population model to investigate the combined effects of variability in temperature and environmental factors such as food availability on population productivity. These simulations are used to understand the combined impacts of climate and other environmental variability changes on fishery assessments and management.
7667: Shellfish beds perform a number of ecosystem functions disproportionate to their size. Anthropogenic activities have degraded these populations and sparked interest in their restoration. Population connectivity determines if restored populations are sustainable through self-recruitment or larval supply from alternate source populations. This study investigated larval dispersal of green lipped mussels, Perna canaliculus, from aquaculture sites in the Firth of Thames (FoT). This species was once abundant in the area, however currently the largest known populations of P. canaliculus in the FoT are in aquaculture operations. A biophysical particle tracking model was used to determine potential larval dispersal pathways from aquaculture sites. Results were then compared to a shell microchemistry study which empirically estimated the natal origin of recent settlers at sites throughout the area. The model showed that larvae can settle throughout the FoT. Larvae originating from only a few sites are likely to dominate settlement in the area due to high larval production at these sites. Shell microchemistry suggested recent settlers originated throughout the study area supporting the results of modelling. These results suggest that larvae produced at aquaculture may contribute to a well-mixed larval pool which may settle throughout the FoT and potentially contribute to population recovery.

The University of Auckland - Institute of Marine Science; NIWA
7668: The recent Environment Aotearoa 2019 report identified climate change as a priority issue already affecting New Zealand. The report was prepared by the Ministry for the Environment (MfE) and Stats NZ under the Environmental Reporting programme to provide New Zealanders with independent information on our environment. The report is supported by long-term national indicators of ocean changes; including indicators on sea surface temperature, sea level rise, ocean waves, ocean acidification and primary productivity. MfE and StatsNZ are committed (and legislated) to maintain long-term reporting for our oceans. The upcoming marine domain report published this October will update our most recent understanding of long term climate trends and related impacts. In response to these environment reports MfE is involved in several initiatives including the 2017 Coastal Hazards and Climate Change – Guidance for Local Government in New Zealand to help local government and others assess, plan for, and manage the increasing risks facing coastal communities. Together with other agencies and stakeholders MfE is also developing an Ocean Acidification Action Plan for New Zealand.
7669: Global demand for protein is putting increasing pressure on fisheries resources. Fishing practices such as trawling are commonly used, and there is growing public and market awareness of potential environmental impacts that arise from these practices. There is scope for improvement by reducing bycatch (fish, seabird, and mammal), reducing seabed impacts, and reducing carbon emissions. In a collaborative transdisciplinary research programme we drew on knowledge and resources from Mātauranga Māori, Western science, fishing and technological expertise to explore new fishing options. Mātauranga Māori-originating harvest methods such as tāruke (pots) offer a way to efficiently target chosen fish species, with minimal impact on non-target species and on the environment. We present work done with two example species, the NZ Scampi Metanephrops challengeri and the ling Genypterus blacodes. "Mau tonu te au kakara i te moana" (So that the sweet scent of the ocean remains)
7670: Spatial genetic data suggest that the race to colonize new space following a physical disturbance event can lead to profound and long-lasting spatial structuring of biodiversity. Recent and historic tectonic uplift of New Zealand shores presents unrivaled opportunities to understand the marine biological impacts of sudden geological disturbance. Our study area is a 23 km stretch of prehistorically-uplifted rocky intertidal coast in southern Otago. Topographic features and subfossil data suggest that this coastal region, delineated by the Akatore Fault, was uplifted 3m at 1000-1400 YBP. We hypothesized that this major disturbance drove substantial biodiversity turnover. We focused on contemporary phylogeographic structure of intertidal bull-kelp (Durvillaea antarctica), inferred from 229 COI sequences from 31 localities. We found a sharp genetic discontinuity between samples from within the uplifted rocky shore relative to samples from flanking non-uplifted sites immediately to the northeast and southwest. All localities within the uplifted coasts were dominated by a distinctive kelp haplotype NZS2, a lineage which is restricted to coastlines 30-150 km north of the uplifted zone. Our data show that modern kelp populations retain a striking genetic signature of prehistoric disturbance mediated by coastal uplift which highlights the potentially lasting marine biological effects of coastal earthquake uplift.
Marine Science Department, University of Otago
7671: This presentation discusses the traditional Māori concept of ngā tohu o te taiao or tohu (abbreviated version) which refers to the environmental indicators or signs and signals of the natural world. Tohu are widely used by kaitiaki or Māori environmental practitioners to identify trends or changes in the state or health of marine taonga (culturally treasured) species and their associated environments. Māori worldviews position humans within nature and focuses on ways in which cultural understandings and intergenerational connections between people and their bio-physical contexts assist in the retention and protection of biodiversity and ecologically sustainable ecosystems. Tohu are a fundamental expression of kaitiakitanga or active guardianship and are based on the primal instinct of survival and recognising that in order to survive one must pay attention to the natural signs and signals thoughtfully to manage our food basket and ourselves into the future. This presentation critically discusses ngā tohu o te taiao as an important and meaningful strategy for empowering transdisciplinary research, understandings and management of marine taonga species and spaces for present and future generations.
National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research (NIWA)
MUSA Dive: Marine and Environmental Services
7672: The coastal waters of Auckland are heavily impacted by high levels of eutrophication and sedimentation as a result of runoff, increased effluent and coastal erosion. Ecosystem health depicts the well-being of natural systems under human-induced stress and has been shown to be affected in harbour and estuarine ecosystems in this region. To date, the health of shallow reef ecosystems remains uncertain and for which indicators have not been developed. Annual monitoring of shallow reef ecosystems has been carried out in the Long Bay area since 2007 providing an opportunity to assess variation in the health of these urban reef ecosystems. Spatiotemporal variation in community composition, the density, size and biomass of key-species (e.g. foundation-species and non-indigenous-species) and other health indicators (e.g. primary production and various diversity measures) was examined and the relationship with environmental variables explored. Most indicators varied between sites and over time. While the reef communities did not exhibit any large-scale changes in structure and composition, some clear trends were detected. There was a general decline in the height of canopy forming algae and dramatic declines in total gastropod densities. While these results suggest a decline in ecosystem health, the underlying drivers of these changes require further investigation.

7673: The 2016 earthquakes in North Canterbury, New Zealand, resulted in massive coastal uplift that partially or wholly extirpated some intertidal bull-kelp and invertebrate populations. This catastrophic disturbance could, however, create opportunities for new genetic lineages of keystone species to establish. We collected beach-cast rafts of habitat-forming species of southern-bull kelp, Durvillaea antarctica and D. poha, along the uplifted North Canterbury coast in 2017 and 2018, to characterise the pool of potential post-disturbance colonists reaching the area. Raft source locations were determined via genome-wide SNP data generated by genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS), with samples from attached populations throughout the species' ranges for reference. Our findings revealed that a number of rafts from both species came from distant lineages, some from southern New Zealand, and some from the west coast or the sub-Antarctic, more than 1200 km away. These results show that diverse lineages are poised to compete for new space in the wake of the quake, highlighting the importance of long-distance dispersal as a mechanism for species to take advantage of environmental change. Furthermore, they demonstrate that high-resolution genomic analyses can, when established populations have been well sampled, be used to determine the provenance of dispersing taxa.
The Australian National University; University of Otago
7674: Ecosystem models are useful for many reasons: they can help to understand how a system is structured, they can suggest future trajectories of change in response to environmental and anthropological drivers, and they can provide guidance on selecting useful ecological indicators. However, ecosystem models come with considerable uncertainty and this uncertainty has led many to question their management value. In this presentation we show how stable isotopes can help to reduce the uncertainty associated with establishing food-web structure in marine ecosystem models. Most food-web models are based on balancing mass-flows across a network. Initial values for model parameters are usually determined from survey and literature data, and then the model is balanced by adjusting parameters. This adjustment is often carried out in an ad-hoc and subjective way, and sometimes by adjusting only certain, poorly-constrained parameters. First, we recognise that the balanced trophic model is highly under-constrained. This means that there is a large family of possible solutions all of which are feasible (to some degree) according to the conceptual framework and available empirical data. Second, we show how stable isotopes can help to explore the "feasible parameter space" and provide estimates of uncertainty on ecosystem properties derived from them.
7675: Submarine canyons potentially concentrate mid-trophic level prey providing enhanced foraging opportunities for marine mammals such as New Zealand fur seals. Although mesopelagic fish and squid constitute an important part of fur seal diet, the overlap between mesopelagic biomass and fur seal distribution is yet to be quantified. To address this, we conducted visual line-transect surveys (n = 8) over the Otago submarine canyons in each of winter 2018 and summer 2019. Along with surface oceanographic data, we also recorded water-column acoustic backscatter (assumed to be a proxy for mid-trophic level biomass) using a 38 kHz scientific echosounder concurrently with the visual survey. We completed 272 km of survey effort, with eight sightings of fur seals in winter compared to 94 in summer, potentially reflecting seasonal differences in foraging distribution. Counts of fur seals per 1km survey segment during summer were related to bathymetric, oceanographic and prey variables via generalised additive models. The best model (32% deviance explained) indicated a negative relationship with distance to the coastline, and positive relationships with SST gradient and epipelagic and mesopelagic backscatter. Our results suggest that submarine canyons modify the availability of pelagic biomass and hence influence the distribution of foraging fur seals.
University of Otago; Yellow-eyed Penguin Trust
7676: Oceanic travel, vessel movement and the transportation of goods at an international scale frequently introduces non-indigenous species into new environments, threatening the native marine biodiversity of many coastline countries. Within the marine environment, space is a limiting resource, resulting in competition for substrate to be intense and fast. Colonial biofouling organisms often rely on their outer surfaces for critical functions such as nutrient and waste exchange, thus, a species ability to compete is often cited as being one if the strongest determinants of success. I will be exploring the evolutionary response of defence chemical release seen in Bryozoans (moss animals), with the hypothesis that non-indigenous species are better competitors and therefore more successful invaders. We hypothesise that specialised allelochemistry confers extreme competitive benefit to marine biofouling invaders through differential effects on native larval settlement. This project will use ex situ colony manipulation and larval dosing experiments to illustrate the role that evolutionary exposure plays in community assembly by examining the differences in native vs introduced species' allelochemistry. This research will be the first of its kind to link introduced species' success to their unique chemistry while simultaneously illustrating how introduced species have a differential effect on native larval settlement choice and success. Findings will illustrate the competitive power of invasive bryozoan species, contributing to scientific and practical knowledge of post-border invasive settlement.
7677: The Cosy Dell site near Gore, Southland (~25 million years old, Late Oligocene) preserves a marine biota that occupied subtropical shallow waters along a coastline of rocky shores, estuaries and sandy beaches, adjacent to a landmass festooned with rainforest and mangroves. The vertebrate assemblage includes penguins, rays, sharks, bony fish, and presumed cetacean, sea bird and sea turtle remains. Specimens are isolated and generally fragmentary, due to the active wave-dominated depositional setting. Teleost otoliths include rock cod, stargazers, opalfishes, grunts, pearlfishes, seabream, hoki, roughy, conger eels and sardines. Chondrichthyan teeth include sand tigers (Odontaspididae), a houndshark (Triakidae) and eagle rays (Myliobatidae). Bones from different-sized penguin species are present, although none are complete enough to be named to genus. Bone dimensions indicate specimens ranging from modern Aptenodytes to Eudyptula in size – encompassing the whole size range of extant Spheniscidae. Small ancient penguins, like their modern counterparts, probably had restricted foraging ranges, and likely exploited local marginal shallow seas. Larger penguins probably foraged in deeper continental shelf and slope waters further afield. The Cosy Dell biota provides unique insights into a rarely-preserved shallow marine paleoecosystem – helping construct a food web of the coastal seas around a warmer ancient southern Zealandia.
