7678: We collected reef shark population data from a large network of no-take and no-entry reserves (i.e. human exclusion areas), as well as from fished reefs, in one of the world's most intensively managed marine parks – the Great Barrier Reef of Australia. The sampled reserves have been protected for varying lengths of time, making it possible to use space-for-time chronosequences to infer recovery trajectories of reef shark populations after extractive use is banned, and to compare the effectiveness of shark population recovery in no-take and no-entry reserves. After 20–40 years of protection, density and biomass of sharks in no-entry reserves approached asymptotes (i.e. plateaus) that were more than double and triple, respectively, those in no-take reserves. These results not only indicate that restoration of near-natural shark populations requires multidecadal time frames, but also clearly demonstrate the superior performance of no-entry reserves in terms of rebuilding shark populations. Given the ubiquitous use of no-take reserves as ecological baselines and the potentially pervasive trophic effects of removing large predators, we argue that current perceptions of the structure and function of natural reef ecosystems may be skewed, which has broad implications for science and management of marine ecosystems.
Reef HQ, Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority
7679: Information from a number of sources, including climate monitoring and population dynamics modelling of fish and marine megafauna populations, suggest there have been major shifts in the ocean climate of New Zealand's Sub-Antarctic region since the 1970s. A new project is undertaking a meta-analysis of information for identifying ocean climate changes in the New Zealand Sub-Antarctic region, including: atmospheric/ocean climate indices, and indices of productivity for primary producers, mesopelagic species, key fish populations, marine mammals and seabirds. This analysis will then inform the development of a multi-species spatial assessment model for understanding the effects of environmental variability and change affecting the function of New Zealand's Sub-Antarctic marine ecosystem.
7680: Sex changing fish provide convenient models to better understand sexual plasticity and cell fate in vertebrates. The precise mechanisms regulating gonadal restructure in fish are not yet understood. Social structure is often an important factor in protogynous species. The removal of a dominant male will often induce sex change in a female member of the same breeding group. Previous studies have demonstrated the significance of both behaviour and the key hormones that regulate the reproductive axis during sex change. However, there is little information regarding the influence of epigenetic mechanisms in this process. DNA methylation silences gene expression by preventing transcription at promoter regions and may regulate key pathways within the reproductive axis. This study seeks to determine whether DNA methylation influences social interactions and sex change in the endemic protogynous wrasse, Notolabrus celidotus. DNA methylation will be chemically inhibited in female fish held in an environment that is socially permissive to sex change. Sham treated control fish will be provided similar conditions. The results of this study will help determine the existence of epigenetic effects in sex change and may elucidate regulatory points within the reproductive axis.
University of Waikato; Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology
7681: Toheroa (Paphies ventricosa), have a distribution unlike that of any other New Zealand marine organism. In the North Island toheroa occur on the west coast of Northland and Horowhenua and in the South Island they are found on beaches south of Invercargill. They are absent from large stretches of coast in between. Genetic data suggest that translocation and seeding of toheroa from northern to southern New Zealand may account for this unusual distribution. In this talk we present the results of an interdisciplinary study which tests the hypothesis that a history of human-mediated translocations have determined the present-day distribution of this taonga (treasured) species. By incorporating Māori environmental knowledge alongside methods from archaeology, ecology and anthropology we hope to unravel the history of New Zealand's most mysterious mollusc, generate knowledge to support the recovery of this iconic species and provide a template for future endeavours where indigenous knowledge is integrated with Western science to address contemporary environmental issues.
7682: Estuaries are a vital and productive part of the New Zealand coastline, where infaunal shellfish are key drivers of ecosystem services (ES) that benefit society. The supply of ES is derived from multiple, interacting ecological functions (EF) and processes, that can vary spatially and temporally due to variation in underlying biophysical structures and patchiness in shellfish distribution. Our work has focussed on quantifying multiple services provided by infaunal filter-feeding shellfish through effects on water clarity, nutrient recycling, and nitrogen removal. To quantify service delivery, we conducted benthic incubations over natural density gradients of Austrovenus stutchburyi on intertidal sandflats, and Paphies australis in subtidal channels. Results indicate density-dependent differences in productivity and nutrient fluxes during light and dark incubations and strong differences between the two habitats. By linking bivalve species, their population structure, processes and functions, to the delivery of ES, we can elucidate the mechanisms underpinning services, and improve our understanding of spatial variation in service supply. Quantifying multiple services simultaneously will improve our ability to inform sustainable use of natural resources and help direct management and restoration efforts.
National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research
National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research; Waikato Regional Council
7683: Light is an essential for photosynthetic organisms including seaweeds. During periods of low photon flux density they can acclimate, but during the transition their growth is likely to be unbalanced. Expressing growth in different measures of biomass allows direct comparisons to be made because all the values have the same units. Ulva pertusa was cultivated for 30 days in chambers with constant water flow and submitted to different percentages of ambient light. They were weighed, trimmed and samples for chlorophyll (Chl), fresh (FW), dry (DW), ash-free dry weight (AFDW) and surface area were taken. Mean maximum growth rate was 0.20 d-1 and growth was zero below 6.1% ambient light. Total chlorophyll at 100% ambient light remained steady throughout the experiment (3.9 mg g-1 DW). For the 10% treatment there was a marked increase over the first 7 days (11.6 mg g-1 DW). In the control, all growth rates presented balanced growth. During the 3 to 7 day the chlorophyll increase was 0.32 d-1. During steady-state (21-31 days) the chlorophyll and AFDW growth rates were 30% higher. This suggest that chlorophyll and organic matter were increasing at a faster rate than the FW, and area was increasing at a slower rate.
7684: Biomonitoring provides a mechanism for assessing the biochemical health of the marine environment as potentially toxic trace metals are taken up by organisms that become recorders of their chemical environment. Importantly, it reflects the bio-available fraction of metals in the environment and their uptake into different levels of the food chain. An ongoing baseline project of New Zealand's coastal and deep ocean has found that both amphipods and decapods (crabs and lobsters) are useful indicators of their marine environment when compared across sites and, ultimately, over time. Analysis of 30 trace elements using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry allows to evaluate natural variations among localities and effects of parameters such as specimen size, trophic level or tissue type. We are investigating the variability in the accumulation of metals between eight species, including the New Zealand crayfish, between sites around the country, and in a time series through a doping study. We aim to equip a New Zealand biomonitoring toolbox with tools to prepare us for future questions such as changes in levels of trace metals resulting from human activities such as offshore mining activities, urban development, or ocean acidification.
School of Geography, Environment & Earth Science, Victoria University of Wellington
School of Biological Science, Victoria University of Wellington
School of Geography, Environment & Earth Science, Victoria University of Wellington
School of Biological Science, Victoria University of Wellington
7685: Green-lipped mussels (Perna canaliculus) are important suspension feeding bivalves, supporting ecosystem functioning in a variety of ways. Filter-feeding mussels effectively remove phytoplankton from the water column and deposit unused organic material to the seafloor as feces and pseudofeces. These biodeposits enhance the microbially-mediated removal of nitrogen from surrounding sediments through a process termed denitrification. The historic collapse of green-lipped mussel beds in the 1960s is associated with a loss of services in coastal environments. In response, restoration groups have dispersed over 100 T of mussels throughout the Gulf, creating restored populations capable of influencing nitrogen cycling in benthic soft sediments. Mussels at each site have self-aggregated into various spatial formations (e.g. small clumps vs. densely packed beds), also affecting denitrification rates. This project examines the effect of mussel spatial arrangement on denitrification, with field sites providing an experimental gradient over which to explore changes in nutrient cycling under varying environmental conditions. Results show that nitrogen removal is generally enhanced in the presence of mussels, but is altered by spatial arrangement and environmental factors. This research is first in exploring the effects of bivalve spatial heterogeneity on denitrification, providing quantitative justification for restoration projects, and aiding in future restoration project design.
7686: Microplastic pollution is generally regarded as ubiquitous throughout the marine environment, however the extent of its abundance and distribution within parts of the Southern Hemisphere – including New Zealand and the Southern Ocean – is relatively unknown. The aim of this study is to assess within-year and between-year variation of this pollutant along a transect between New Zealand and the Ross Sea, through use of a 9-year time series dataset obtained by NIWA (2009-2018). A Continuous Plankton Recorder (CPR) was used to sample surface waters for zooplankton and incidental microplastic debris throughout 7 oceanographic zones South of New Zealand, totalling approximately 4,000 km worth of southward and northward transits per year. Individual samples were then visually analysed: particle size, colour, type, oceanographic zone, and associated zooplankton abundance were recorded. Preliminary results demonstrate that microplastic particles within the Southern Ocean are largely composed of synthetic fibres, as opposed to beads or fragments. Expected results include a decreasing abundance of microplastic particles with increasing distance from New Zealand waters and an increase in overall microplastic pollution throughout the years. There is also the possibility of a correlation between the abundance of zooplankton and microplastic debris.
School of Biological Sciences, Victoria University of Wellington
School of Biological Sciences, Victoria University of Wellington
7687: Marine heatwaves are increasing globally and New Zealand has seen some of its most severe marine heatwaves (MHWs) in recent years. However, recent analysis of global trends in marine heatwaves have largely focused on satellite-derived SST data, that are temporally limited and do not necessarily reflect nearshore conditions. While MHWs have received a large amount of media attention, it remains unclear whether they are increasing in New Zealand's coastal waters. We analysed New Zealand's two longest sea surface temperature records to investigate how the intensity, duration and frequency of MHWs has changed over the last 50-60 years. We found a significant increase in the duration and frequency of MHWs in southern New Zealand, whereas there was no evidence of increasing trends in marine heatwave metrics in northern New Zealand. This spatial variation in the long-term trends of marine heatwaves reflects large-scale variation in warming trends around New Zealand, and highlights the complexity of both understanding and predicting the effects of climate change in our coastal waters.
7688: Although shark populations are decreasing in many coral reef habitats, the ecosystem effects of this loss are poorly understood. Rays are prevalent mesopredators in tropical coral reefs that are preyed upon by top predators like sharks. Studies have suggested reduced predator abundances lead to increases in mesopredator abundance. We examined the relationship between predator abundance and behaviour of small rays using baited remote underwater videos (BRUVS) at 19 sites across six countries. Where predators were more abundant, the bluespotted maskray complex (Neotrygon spp.) and two species of ribbon-tailed rays (Taeniura spp.) were sighted less often. Where predators were less abundant, rays spent significantly more time in view, visited BRUVS multiple times, and were more likely to feed from bait bags. In addition to predator abundance, Neotrygon spp. were more abundant on deeper, lower relief BRUVS, while Taeniura spp. were more prevalent in reef associated shallow, high relief BRUVS. Overall, this study demonstrated predator abundance had significant effects on small ray abundance and behaviour. The results also demonstrate that changes in behaviour associated with predator loss may make the interpretation of phenomenon like mesopredator release difficult to define without taking behavioural effects into account.
James Cook University; Australian Institute of Marine Science
7689: All communities rely on infrastructure for effective functioning. Since the 2016 Kaikoura earthquake, the ecological infrastructure of the nearshore zone has been severely compromised through the loss of biogenic habitat, poor recovery of key algal species from loss of population connectivity, and the interaction of altered physical properties of reef topography, waves, temperature, sedimentation and light. Resilience of many species has been poor and recovery slow. Here we discuss these requisites of ecosystems and the prognosis of recovery of communities and functions along the earthquake-affected coastline of the northeastern South Island.
Marine Ecology Research Group, Canterbury University
Marine Ecology Research Group, Canterbury University
Marine Ecology Research Group, Canterbury University
7690: Ecosystem multifunctionality is defined as the performance of multiple ecosystem functions simultaneously. It is an alternative concept to commonly used single-function approach, where functions are measured in isolation. Through the concept of ecosystem multifunctionality we can more accurately establish the relationships within an ecosystem, e.g. link multiple species and their trait assemblages to the multiple ecosystem functions. This task, however, is difficult as the relationships between ecosystem components are highly complex. Current approaches to studying multifunctionality suffer from shortcomings that oversimplify these relationships, e.g. require adding or averaging of functions, risking important messages to be lost. New tools are, therefore, needed and in this study we to introduce Bayesian Belief Network (BN) analysis to ecosystem multifunctionality research. BN, using the combination of expert knowledge and field data, allows to quantify changes in ecosystem multifunctionality from increasing nitrogen levels (0g Nm-2, 150g Nm-2, 600 g Nm-2) added to the system. The experiment was conducted in intertidal sandflat Kaipara Harbour, NZ. The results demonstrate that the loss of species and subsequent loss in functional traits resulted in multifunctionality trade-offs, i.e. changes in performance across a number of ecosystem functions including N release, denitrification, primary production, sediment formation and stability and carbon sequestration.
7691: An individual-based model was used to analyse Maui dolphin movements and distribution. Simulated dolphin movements were compared with field data. Distance moved per hour follows a Poisson distribution which the scaling exponent µ. Depth preference follows a sigmoid function: (1 + 0.011-d/δ)-1 where d is water depth (in metres) and δ is the depth-preference exponent. Dolphins move to a new location with preference = 1 if there are no dolphins present and 1+ σ if there are other dolphins present. The resulting maps of Maui dolphin distribution show considerable overlap with gillnet and trawl fisheries. We recommend adjusting the boundaries for protected areas in which gillnets and/or trawling is banned, to provide more effective protection. Recommendations by the International Whaling Commission (IWC) and IUCN are included in the set of management options. The IWC has recommended extending protection to 20 nautical miles offshore for Maui dolphins. The IUCN has recommended extending protection to the 100 metre depth contour for both Maui and Hector's dolphins. The New Zealand government is currently considering improvements to the protection of Maui and Hector's dolphins, with a decision expected in August 2019.
Wageningen University; Netherlands Institute for Ecological Research
7692: Global demand for octopus as seafood has been increasing but is now unable to be fully met from wild fisheries. Establishing octopus aquaculture would help to meet the global demand and reduce fishing pressure on wild populations. However, rearing larvae of various species of octopus has proven to be extremely challenging. Larval rearing and feeding behaviour in Octopus tetricus was examined in this study to describe larval development and also to attempt to incubate octopus eggs without a female. Hatching success of over 90% was achieved in upwelling systems with added aeration. Food particle capture success of newly-hatched larvae increase from 0 dph (days post hatch) to 2 dph and drop off until 5 dph when all larvae were dead. The highest capture success of 38% was observed when artificial diets were presented, compared to 31% with live brine shrimp. Our results demonstrate that high egg survival can be achieved without a grooming female and artificial diets are possible alternatives to live prey for newly hatched larvae. These results are encouraging in the further development of octopus aquaculture. However, more research is needed to determine who much of the artificial diet was ingested and which diet features are most suitable.
7693: The intensification of farming and shoreline development is increasing the discharge of nutrients to coastal environments and the occurrence of primary and secondary eutrophication symptoms in New Zealand's estuaries. Estuarine sediments and the residing macrofaunal communities are key drivers in ecosystem functioning, which influences the exchange and transformation of nutrients. As benthic communities are modified by eutrophic symptoms, the effects on ecosystem functioning may also change. In this study, we used a eutrophication gradient approach to explore changes in ecosystem functioning in Waihī Estuary, Bay of Plenty. Seven sites were selected based on visual signs of impact, including percentage Gracilaria (red algae) cover, sediment oxygen depth and mud content. During summer 2018, five paired light and dark benthic flux chambers (0.25 m2), approximately 37 L in volume, were deployed at each site to measure inorganic nutrient and oxygen fluxes across the sediment-water interface. Sites were characterised and compared by quantifying the macrofaunal community, sediment grain size, organic matter content, and chlorophyll a and pore water concentrations. Here we will examine the dynamics of changes in community structure across the eutrophication gradient and the influence this has on ecosystem function.

7694: Fisheries outside national EEZs are managed by regional bodies with international membership. The South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation (SPRFMO) manages non-highly migratory fisheries in the South Pacific, including New Zealand and Australian bottom trawl fisheries for deep-water species. New Zealand officials and scientists have been collaborating with Australia, Chile, and the EU on the development of a revised management measures for bottom fisheries. As part of this process, officials, scientists and stakeholders engaged in a series of ten formal workshops between 2016 and 2018 to agree data and settings for decision-support tools and to develop options for spatial management areas. The final proposed management areas adopted by the SPRFMO Commission in early 2019, had substantially better performance than existing measures in terms of protecting vulnerable marine ecosystems and providing access for the fishery. We discuss the advantages of using quantitative decision support tools to assemble and interrogate available information to engage diverse stakeholders in processes that encourage them to state their objectives for management and appreciate those of others. Working in this way, stakeholders can understand and consider the trade-offs inherent in most resource management decisions and focus their energies on issues that really matter.

7695: Species classifications have the advantage of summarising complex multi-species data in a reduced set of layers that describe broad patterns in species diversity providing a common currency for discussions across different resource users. These classifications can be created at various scales (e.g. 5 to 500+); particularly useful when considering conservation planning at differing spatial scales (regional – international). The systematic conservation planning software Zonation was used to explore the efficiency of using a recently developed Gradient Forest (GF) classification of demersal fish species in systematic conservation planning compared to the 'usual' approach of using individual species distribution layers. Multiple practicalities for using such classifications in conservation planning were tested, including: investigating the effect of classification group number, the use of inter- and intra-group similarity (a practical way of incorporating beta diversity), the use of species richness (alpha diversity) and the effect of different weightings of these layers. The choice of strategy and parameterisation of the analysis used in application of environmental surrogates to conservation prioritization had a considerable effect on the quality of the outcome. The performance of the analysis ranged from poor (random prioritisation) to near-optimal (use of inter- and intra-group similarity and species richness with optimum weighting).
7696: Environmental challenges, society and technology are changing dramatically – and all at once. What does this mean with respect to the underpinning understanding of the shelf seas surrounding New Zealand/Aotearoa. These seas, nominally extending out to the 250 m depth contour, are complex and varied. A recent review summarizes the present state of knowledge of the physical processes that control ocean transport and mixing in this domain – thus forming the basis for much of the marine science so vital to stakeholders in the widest sense. The focus of a recent review of this science was on recent regional advances in understanding the balance between off-shelf drivers, terrestrially sourced freshwater, winds, tides, stratification and the underlying topography. Here we summarize the review and examine outstanding themes such as connectivity, climate and stratification. We will close with an assessment of the potential future for understanding the physical marine environment of the shelf seas of the New Zealand region in this changing world.
7697: Global climate shifts are having profound effects on oceanographic and atmospheric conditions, yet understanding the consequences on marine ecosystems is limited by our inability to observe changes to biota on relevant scales. Localised stressors such as sedimentation and eutrophication can compound global stressors, but linking disparate scales of stressors temporally and spatially is challenging. Earth-oriented satellites such as MODIS-Aqua provide frequent broad-scale images across multiple spectral bands, allowing the calculation of several biophysical products, but suffer from low pixel resolution and atmospheric occlusion. It is possible to overcome these limitations using aircraft equipped with multispectral imaging sensors to target biogenic features of interest and separate multiple functional groups of marine vegetation. Here we discuss the use of multiple scales of remote sensing to monitor, manage and disentangle the relative effects of local and global stressors on coastal ecosystems, focussing on rocky reefs. We show examples of declining cover of kelp in southern New Zealand, strongly linked to marine heat wave events. Integrating multiple scales of remotely sensed data from drones-planes-satellites is proving valuable in detecting changes to vulnerable biogenic habitats and in assessing the relative influence of global (e.g., rising temperature) and local (e.g., sedimentation, fishing) stressors on declining biota.
7698: Estuaries are hotspots for biogeochemical cycling. Underpinning biogeochemical cycling within estuarine sediments is the bacterial community. Bacteria through the release of extracellular enzymes break down organic matter within the sediment driving the carbon cycle and nutrient regeneration in the sediments. There are limited studies looking into the factors controlling enzyme activity within estuarine sediments and how anthropogenic stressors may influence this relationship. Our study aims to look at how a changing sedimentary gradient and nutrient enrichment influences enzyme activity and therefore carbon and nutrient cycling within estuaries. Understanding how enzyme activity may change under increasing nutrient enrichment across sedimentary gradients is important as with increasing anthropogenic stressors these key ecosystem functions driven by enzyme activity may start to change and estuarine health may reduce. An in situ manipulative experiment using nutrient addition across a sedimentary gradient was set up and sedimentary enzyme activity was measured as a proxy for organic matter breakdown and nutrient regeneration. Initial results show that mud content, bivalve and macrofaunal activity are the major drivers of enzyme activity within the study estuaries.
7699: We previously documented how earthquake-induced seismic uplift (north of 42.51° S) and marine heatwaves (south of 42.51° S) affected populations of southern bull kelp on the South Island of New Zealand. To date, however, we have only examined these impacts in isolation. Here, we consider how bull kelp responded to cascading effects of the November 2016 seismic uplift followed by the hot summers of 2017/18 and 2018/19. Analyses indicated a relationship between pre-earthquake latitudinal and vertical distribution patterns and stress-impacts. Of the southern bull kelp species found on mainland New Zealand rocky reefs (Durvillaea antarctica, D. willana and D. poha), D. poha was most heavily affected. Durvillaea poha is the most range-restricted species with the most southerly northern distribution limit and typically co-occurs with D. antarctica but at higher tidal elevation than D. willana. We speculate that the interaction between D. poha's adaptation to cooler waters and intertidal stressors (desiccation, heat) may exacerbate deleterious impacts on it. Given predicted future increases in oceanic warming and marine heatwaves, it is likely that D. poha will be greatly diminished and even locally extinct where thermal hot spots persist. We discuss the implications of the potential loss of this iconic intertidal foundation species.

7700: Marine microbes are key players in marine ecosystems, driving the cycling of energy and matter. Understanding the factors that influence the microbial community structure is therefore critical. Systems with strong horizontal and vertical gradients, i.e. fjords, are useful in studying the response of microbial communities to environmental factors. Gradients such as a fjord's low salinity layer (LSL), are expected to drive microbial (prokaryotic and eukaryotic) communities. This study, the first to utilise both 16S and 18S amplicon sequencing, assesses changes in Next Generation Sequencing derived microbial community patterns (From Fiordland, NZ) associated with the LSL and underlying seawater in multiple fjords, and other environmental parameters. Marine water samples were collected from the surface and deep water at multiple stations along the length of six fjords. We found that depth, amongst the environmental variables examined, showed the strongest correlation with patterns in microbial diversity and community structure. Horizontal community changes were also observed due to differences in community structure changes along the horizontal axis of individual fjords. Changes in prokaryotic communities coincided with changes in eukaryotic communities. Depth, through direct or indirect effects, seems to be the main factor controlling Fiordland's prokaryotic and eukaryotic richness, community diversity and taxonomic composition patterns.

7701: Foundational organisms form structurally complex habitats in multiple coastal ecosystems. However, habitat complexity comprises several interrelated attributes, such as number, size, and spatial arrangement of complexity-forming elements. Understanding the roles of these attributes in determining how associated organisms use biogenic habitats remains an elusive task. Here, we assessed the relationships between several structural-complexity attributes of the kelp Lessonia trabeculata and the abundance and distribution of egg depositions by Schroederichthys chilensis. Over 1 yr, we conducted seasonal SCUBA surveys of egg capsule depositions across individual and patch scales. The number of eggs per kelp was modeled as a function of kelp maximum frond length, holdfast diameter, number of stipes, percentage cover, plant density, and plant aggregation. The analysis of zero-inflated generalized linear models and second-order Akaike's information criterion indicated that the models incorporating maximum frond length and percentage cover consistently showed the best balance between fit and complexity. In general, these attributes were positively, but not necessarily linearly, linked to egg counts. These findings suggest that catsharks select for taller, physically stable, and thicker kelps to deposit egg capsules. Moreover, our results allow us to enhance the accuracy of the definition of shark nursery grounds, a central concept for shark conservation.

7702: Benthic primary producers provide energy and habitat for marine communities, and produce hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), a driver of oxidative stress. Through their high biomass, productivity and alteration of local hydrodynamics, benthic primary producers can potentially increase H₂O₂ concentrations within biogenic structures they form. This study determined that H₂O₂ production by benthic primary producers may act as an external stressor in coastal ecosystems. This was achieved by measuring H₂O₂ concentrations within sea lettuce blooms (Ulva spp.), giant kelp forests (Macrocystis pyrifera), and seagrass meadows (Zostera muelleri); quantifying H₂O₂ production rates of these species; and testing heterotrophic bacterial response to relevant H₂O₂ concentrations. Ulva spp. produced five-times more H₂O₂ than other species, with concentrations higher within Ulva blooms than seagrass meadows and kelp forests, where H₂O₂ concentrations were not above ambient. At in-situ concentrations, H₂O₂ inhibited bacterial production and carbon flow through the microbial loop by 75-99%. This study reveals H₂O₂ as an additional stressor in Ulva spp. blooms and identifies low H₂O₂ production rates and retention around biogenic structures as positive attributes of M. pyrifera and Z. mulleri. H₂O₂ production by benthic primary producers may affect carbon flow through the microbial loop, thus propagating a stress signal up the food web.
7703: The vast majority of global trade is transported via maritime shipping. Along with intended cargo, ships transport non-indigenous, potentially harmful species (NIS) via ballast water and hull biofouling. Each type of cargo ship has a different profile of marine biosecurity risk due to ballast tank size and number, hull configuration, and other factors. Each type of globally traded commodity can be associated with the most likely ship type used to transport it. Each pair of global trade partners (countries) also has a different probability for successful translocation and establishment of NIS from one to the other based on geographic distance, environmental compatibility, and voyage conditions. Multi-region input-output analysis, a method from economics, can be used to estimate the magnitude of seaborne trade connections between individual countries based on physical volume of commodity traded. In this study, by linking ship type to volume of commodity traded by commodity type, and accounting for establishment probability between source and destination, the magnitude of marine biosecurity risk will be deduced from the magnitude of seaborne trade connections.
7704: This project aimed to evaluate the effects of mussel farming on Hector's dolphins through passive acoustic monitoring using T-PODs. These devices record the occurrence and timing of odontocete echolocation clicks. Six bays were studied from 2018 to 2019; three with mussel farms (Menzies Bay, Pigeon Bay, Port Levy) and three without (Little Akaroa, Decanter Bay, Little Port Cooper). In bays with farms, T-POD was moored by the farm and the opposite side of the bay. Bays without farms had T-POD in the centre for small bays and both sides of the bay in Little Akaloa. T-PODs recorded for between 12 - 29 days in each location, resulting in 598 days of data in total. Detections were summarised as dolphin positive minutes per day and compared using ANOVA. Data showed dolphin detections in all bays on ≥75% of days sampled. There were significant differences in dolphin detections between bays, but no consistent effect of mussel farms. Bays with farms had lower rates of detections adjacent to farms, compared with opposite side. This study suggests that mussel farms have impacts on the environment of Hector's dolphins. Their effects should be considered in future management of the habitat of this endangered species.
7705: What if protecting one endemic threatened species meant culling another native protected species? How should that decision be made? What if there were no scientific data informing that decision-making process? At Ripiro Beach (Northland), once the site of the largest toheroa (Paphies ventricosa) population, the South Island Pied Oystercatcher (SIPO, Haemotopus ostralegus finschi), a natural predator of toheroa, has been blamed for their continuing decline. There are even calls to cull SIPO populations to protect toheroa. At present there is no science to inform the decision-making. This study aims to investigate SIPO predation on toheroa at Ripiro Beach. The objectives are to identify: 1) spatial and temporal foraging patterns of SIPOs, 2) what size-class of toheroa they are predominantly feeding on, and 3) their predation success rate, as a proxy measure of the birds' potential impact on local toheroa populations. Results will be used to address existing knowledge gaps surrounding the perceived interspecific conflict and inform discussion on the management of the two endemic New Zealand species.
7706: There is little known about the ecology of deep-sea benthic ecosystems, yet these habitats are increasingly disturbed by modern fishing activities. Unravelling the diet of deep-sea benthic species can shed light on the ecology of these ecosystems. New Zealand scampi (Metanephrops challengeri) are a lucrative benthic lobster species and samples for this study were collected by commercial trawlers from four dispersed locations between 100 m and 1100 m depth. This research used next-generation sequencing to analyse the diet of these deep-sea lobsters by using DNA metabarcoding methods on gut contents recovered from the samples. Over 30 different food items were identified in the diet and the composition of the diet differed among locations. The diet of scampi included sea stars, octopuses, copepods and seals! The results provide not only insight into the scampi diet, but also help to determine its position in the deep-sea benthic community's food web. The diet indicates that scampi are primarily opportunistic scavengers with a large proportion of their food material likely to be already dead and settled out of the water column onto the seafloor.
7707: The Ross Sea Region Marine Protected Area (RSRMPA) came into effect in December 2017 following a decade of work building consensus on its objectives and boundaries among Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) members. A research and monitoring plan was developed that included five-yearly reports on the science being conducted by CCAMLR members to ensure that these objectives and boundaries were being achieved, and still relevant, over the 35 year life-span of the RSRMPA. Based on data submitted to the CCAMLR Secretariat, I present preliminary results on the scientific effort of members as they relate to the RSRMPA objectives under three distinct research categories (reference areas, threat mitigation, representativeness), highlighting New Zealand's contribution relative to other countries. I also discuss how these research efforts will be used to evaluate the RSRMPA objectives and boundaries, using key examples from New Zealand research, before highlighting potential knowledge gaps for the future.
7708: Long-term time series observations provide valuable data that is crucial to understanding natural processes and detecting ecosystem changes. The Munida Time Series is a repeat oceanographic transect off the southeast coast of New Zealand that spans the narrow continental shelf. It is the longest running data record of ocean carbonate chemistry in the southern hemisphere and it uniquely passes through three distinct water masses: neritic nearshore waters, the subtropical waters of the Southland Current, and subantactic waters off the shelf break. This time series has been able to document the decline in surface ocean pH consistent with increasing atmospheric CO2 in a process called ocean acidification. The factors controlling the variability in the seasonal carbon cycle in the subantarctic surface waters of the SW Pacific were previously assessed using the initial 10 years of data record. Here, we present an update over the last two decades and discuss the drivers controlling pH and pCO2 in the SW Pacific Ocean and the trends that have occurred as a result of climate change and ocean acidification.
7709: Estuaries are dynamic ecosystems serving as the interface between the terrestrial and marine environments. Steep biogeochemical gradients and high productivity make estuarine habitats some of the world's most ecologically and economically valuable ecosystems. However, their location also makes estuaries vulnerable to anthropogenic stressors. Perhaps the most critical stressor in New Zealand is the increase of sediment deposition in estuaries. Land use change in coastal areas, as well as sea level rise, are increasing rates of erosion and terrestrial sediment transport to estuaries. This increase in sediment load decreases water clarity and light attenuation to primary producers, and alters the carbon supplied to intertidal sediments. As sand flats transition to mud flats there is a cascade of co-varying shits in ecosystem functions. The aim of this study was to further understand these shifts in respond to increasing sedimentation. Using in situ measurements we constructed a network of ecosystem functions which highlight key interactions. The goal is to use this network to inform future experiments and models. Preliminary data suggest that muddier sediments have depressed nitrogen removal capacity and significantly altered macrofaunal communities. These changes could have far-reaching consequences for the resilience of estuaries and the delivery of valuable ecosystem services.

7710: Salt marshes are highly productive ecosystems characterized by halotolerant plants that have colonized the high intertidal zone. Unfortunately, most salt marshes in Maritime Canada were converted to agricultural land following European colonisation in the 17th century. However, there is now considerable interest in reverting diked farmland to salt marsh. Managed realignment, where a new dike is built inland and a salt marsh encouraged to develop in front of it, is a popular coastal management strategy in Europe, and was tested here. This salt marsh restoration started in 2010 in New Brunswick, Canada, when dikes protecting two cells of farmland were mechanically breached. Each summer, we quantify the emergent plant and invertebrate communities of these restoration sites and 2 adjacent reference sites. The restoration is currently at a critical phase where (i) the salt marsh foundational grass species, Spartina alterniflora, has established and spread throughout the restoration sites and (ii) the old protective dikes have completely eroded away. Encouragingly, the restoration sites are still accumulating sediment at high rates and shoreline erosion has slowed. This study represents the first managed realignment in Maritime Canada and provides insights on the long-term restoration dynamics of salt marshes in the upper Bay of Fundy.
7711: Ngāti Kurī are an iwi descended from the founding peoples of the northernmost peninsula of Aotearoa. Whilst the iwi itself is relatively small, they have vast areas of ocean and land under their guardianship. This includes the future 'Rangitāhua/Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary' that will protect up to 620,000km2 of NZ's EEZ, and large areas of land, with environmental, cultural and spiritual significance. Ngāti Kurī are committed to working together to achieve community resilience, shared prosperity and self-determination and are mindful of generations of research that have been done in their rohe (tribal lands). Their strategic vision, known as their 'flight path' is a thousand year plan which uses science to add value to intergenerational succession and includes ambitious goals to achieve restoration of biodiversity, both on land and in water. A unique partnership with the Auckland Museum has resulted in a 'Bioblitz' programme that includes successive two-way in-situ wānanga (workshops). This transformational way of working also aims to support the development of Aotearoa into a 'dual heritage' society. Ngāti Kurī has management over their schools, setting the curriculum to fit with their long term strategy. Some dramatic results include educational improvement, empowerment and connectivity amongst the community.
7712: The climate of New Zealand is changing. This has predicted knock on effects for the Coastal Marine Area (CMA) of New Zealand including ocean acidification; sea temperature increases; sea level rises and increased storminess. For local authorities to effectively manage the CMA in this changing world, these authorities need to understand how these effects will impact on regional infrastructure and ecology, compound existing management difficulties in the CMA, and produce new and unexpected challenges. The response by regional authorities to this challenge is mixed, from declarations of a 'climate emergency' to notable silence. In its science strategy (2015) the coastal special interest group (CSIG) determined that understanding the regional impacts of climate change was one of its four goals. This talk will discuss how far the CSIG has travelled in achieving this goal as a collective; and present some case studies of different approaches to tackling climate change issues at a regional level.
7713: Hydrothermal vent habitats represent a very small proportion of the seafloor, yet they host diverse, unique and poorly-known faunas. Due to their formations of high-value poly-metallic deposits, many vent fields are being evaluated for mineral extraction, necessitating an improved understanding of vent communities and population connectivity patterns. Correct taxonomic determination of specimens is important to assay the sensitivity of habitats to exploitation and to accurately quantify patterns of regional connectivity. Restriction of analyses to enigmatic named species or broad genus-level identifications fails to account for the most sensitive taxa: regional endemics. We present a simple genetic dataset of bathymodioline mussels with a focus on the southwest Pacific and discuss what such datasets can tell us about the vulnerability of venting systems and, more importantly, what they cannot.

7714: It is a critical time for the endemic hoiho | yellow-eyed penguin, which is surviving at low levels on the New Zealand mainland. The cumulative impact of numerous marine and terrestrial threats, have led to increased mortalities and reduced breeding success. The hoiho is an unfortunate indicator of the state of our coastal environment. The latest breeding season has been a particularly bad one with an estimated 225 breeding pairs on the mainland, down from 255 last year. Numbers have declined continuously since 2008 (from the mid-1990s onwards there were an estimated 400-600 pairs) and the threat of mainland extinction is very real. Breeding success was very low this season with very few pairs managing to fledge chicks naturally. The season was characterised by a series of adverse events, including two starvation episodes resulting from a changing marine environment, and subsequent disease events. These are in addition to impacts from visitor disturbance, predators, fisheries bycatch and others. Conservation management needs to be dynamic, flexible and adaptable enough to cope with the range and changing nature of the environment and threats facing hoiho. Human intervention is at an all-time high for these birds, without which their future is uncertain.
7715: The biological carbon pump links surface to deep waters while driving global oceanic carbon budgets. Sinking particles from surface waters provide key nutrients to the deep ocean, but also serve as a 'seed bank' for new organisms migrating into the deep ocean. A recent study provided evidence of this surface-deep microbial community composition link via sinking particles. However, the temporal/seasonal variability of surface-deep conectivity remains unexplored. Here, a three year time-series of microbial community composition from the Munida Microbial Observatory Time-Series (MOTS) epipelagic and mesopelagic waters was used to study seasonality of microbial communities. Both showed consistent seasonal patterns, and high variation over time, particularly in surface waters. Most of the seasonal variability in prokaryotic community was associated with phytoplankton bloom periods. Various surface copiotrophic bacteria growing in response to phytoplankton blooms, but not originally present in the mesopelagic, were also found in deep waters after the bloom. Thus, the input of surface prokaryotes into the deep ocean seems a seasonal phenomena linked to the occurrence of phytoplankton blooms. This study further highlights the dynamic nature of deep ocean ecosystems, and the value of time-series datasets to reveal the natural variability that is impossible to capture with single sample analysis.
7716: Mark rate, or the proportion of the population with unique, identifiable marks, must be determined in order to estimate population size from photographic identification data. In this study we address field sampling protocols and estimation methods for robust estimation of mark rate and its uncertainty in cetacean populations. Reliable estimation of mark rate requires an un-biased sampling protocol, such as taking photographs "randomly", i.e., without consideration of whether the individual is marked or not. Sampling theory shows that the sample size of images used to quantify mark rate should be in approximate proportion to the size of the groups photographed. For small groups (<10), taking at least three times as many photographs as there are individuals is a reasonable rule of thumb. Further, in many studies of cetaceans, capture-recapture estimates of abundance are unrealistically precise because uncertainty in mark rate is incorrectly accounted for. The key problem is that images acquired from groups of animals are not a simple random sample. Instead, mark rate and its precision should be quantified using estimators for cluster samples or hierarchical Bayesian modelling. We illustrate these results with a case study on Hector's dolphins (Cephalorhynchus hectori), from Banks Peninsula, New Zealand.
7717: Regional differences in trophic structure and availability of alternate sources of basal organic matter to food webs can affect the volume of organic matter converted into fish biomass. The present study combined stable isotope analyses (δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N) with estimates of biomass density of 22 common reef fishes to compare supply of organic matter derived from macroalgae versus phytoplankton to reef fish communities among 30 sites distributed across Fiordland and the Marlborough Sounds. Fish communities in the Marlborough Sounds were supported by food webs that incorporated less organic matter derived from macroalgae compared to those in Fiordland. Contribution of organic matter derived from macroalgae to fish biomass decreased with trophic level in the Marlborough Sounds, while fishes in Fiordland were supported by a more equal mixture of organic matter derived from phytoplankton and macroalgae. The observed patterns were consistent with limitation in supply of organic matter derived from macroalgae in the Marlborough Sounds, where extensive losses of kelp forest habitat linked to land-based stressors have been reported. The results highlight the importance of considering regional variability in basal organic matter source pools, particularly those produced from sensitive kelp forest habitats, when applying ecosystem-based approaches to managing coastal resources.
7718: The Marine High Risk Site Surveillance (MHRSS) is a national programme of surveys targeted at the early detection of high-risk marine non-indigenous species (NIS). The MHRSS programme, first begun in 2002, involves targeted surveillance undertaken bi-annually at 11 high-risk major ports and marinas around the country. The primary objective of the MHRSS programme is to detect incursions of New to New Zealand marine NIS listed on the Unwanted Organisms Register (Asterias amurensis, Carcinus maenas, Caulerpa taxifolia, Eriocheir sinensis and Potamocorbula amurensis). The MHRSS programme also has two secondary objectives, which are: (i) to detect incursions of marine NIS or cryptogenic organisms not previously recorded in New Zealand, and; (ii) to detect range extensions by marine NIS or cryptogenic organisms that are already established in New Zealand waters (e.g., Arcuatula senhousia, Eudistoma elongatum, Sabella spallanzanii and Styela clava). Here, we present and discuss findings of MHRSS programme for 2018–19, detailing new detections, range extensions, existing invasions, expected detections and surprise ones.

7720: High-throughput sequencing (HTS) technologies are revolutionizing our ability to characterize biodiversity across ecosystems. They offer unprecedented opportunities for new species discovery, ecological trends monitoring, and environmental impact

7722: Light climates in coastal waters are extremely variable in space and time. During winter months low-light periods can last several weeks due to shorter day lengths, increased storm frequencies and rates of sediment transported by rivers. Anthropogenic disturbances like dredging or sediment input from near-shore constructions can add to this natural variability. Consequently, macroalgae growing in near-shore temperate reefs can experience periods of extreme light limitation. Tolerating these conditions requires a certain level of photosynthetic plasticity. As every adjustment comes with a cost, seaweeds acclimating to new light regimes possibly won’t have sufficient energy available for growth or reproduction. Suggesting that the capability to adjust to new conditions drives their occurrence and thereby the individual and community productivity and diversity. Although previous studies explored regulatory and enhancing mechanisms, limitations and pace of adjustments has been barely described. Here, limits of acclimation and recovery to light limitation are investigated comparing common canopy-forming seaweeds found along New Zealand’s rocky shores. Long term, diel observations of photosynthetic parameters paired with fluorescence-based techniques and pigment variability can provide a detailed insight into macroalgal acclimation processes, thresholds and paces and contribute to a better understanding on functionality of habitat-forming seaweeds under light limitation.
National Institute of Water & Atmospheric Research Ltd
7723: To understand the effects of ocean acidification on marine organisms, pH microsensors are widely used to study the biological processes determined by the localised microenvironment. Although most of the present ocean acidification research is based on pH microelectrodes, these electrodes are fragile, expensive, and prone to interference. Our laboratory has developed a new micron-scale pH sensor probe based on optical fibres. One end of the optical fibre is coated in a polymer matrix, which immobilises a colorimetric pH indicator dye while remaining porous enough to allow the target analyte (H3O+) to diffuse into the matrix. A beam of light, which enters at the opposite end of the fibre, passes through the optical fibre and interacts with the polymer matrix. The light is reflected and passes back through the fibre, where a spectra is collected by a detector. Compared to the standard pH microelectrode, this optical sensor is simple to use, insensitive to electromagnetic fields and does not require reference electrode. A field-deployable configuration is being developed, which will allow scientists to conduct in-situ studies into the impact of OA on the microenvironment of marine organisms and ecosystems.

7724: Subtidal mapping can provide context for a wide range of studies. Multibeam and sidescan surveys have been prohibitively expensive and hydrographic survey quality data is often excessive for environmental impact assessments, ecological and biological research. Modern technology has made sounders accessible which are capable of providing quality downscan, sidescan and even multibeam data. At the University of Waikato Coastal Marine Field Station in Tauranga, we have been investigating some methods for recording and applying these types of data to our research.
7725: Rising atmospheric CO₂ levels and the associated decrease in ocean pH has resulted in many changes to the marine environment, with current models predicting CaCO₃ undersaturation in surface waters of the temperate zones by 2100. Of major concern is the effect on coastal marine ecosystems, where the low pH conditions resulting from natural variability are likely to be exacerbated, affecting the growth, construction, and maintenance of CaCO₃ shells and skeletons of many ecologically-important calcifying organisms (e.g. corals, calcifying algae, and molluscs). Currently, efforts to monitor coastal undersaturation events and saturation horizon shoaling are constrained by the need to collect discrete samples for costly and time-consuming laboratory analysis, requiring specialized laboratory technicians and instrumentation. Here, we present the development of a fibre optic-based sensor for the detection of CaCO₃ undersaturation events in seawater. The approach has been adapted into a field deployable sensing system with the goal of supplying a new method of ocean health monitoring.

7726: A new basilosaurid elucidates ontogenetic developmental patterns in Archaeoceti and adds to the range of known Eocene Archaeocetes from New Zealand. This fossil, the “Hurunui Archaeocete”, is from the the Ashley Mudstone of Hurunui, Canterbury (Late Eocene 34.6-39.1 Ma). The slightly disarticulated skeleton is represented by the skull and postcranial bones which consist of a slightly mixed sequence of cervical and thoracic vertebrae and ribs. A juvenile age class is suggested by: open cranial sutures; open sutures in vertebrae leaving the neural arches separate from their corresponding vertebral bodies; in situ teeth fully erupted with an open pulp cavity, the teeth lack abrasive wear apically and lack evident occlusal wear. It is recognised as an archaeocete because the teeth match those of other archaeocetes, as well as tympanoperiotics matching basilosaurids such as Zygorhiza. A cladistic analysis of the skull shows that the fossil is close to Zygorhiza.

7727: The race to colonise new space can generate profound and long-lasting spatial structuring both within and among species. Early-arriving colonists should have an advantage over subsequent dispersers, and once established could effectively block immigration, preventing turnover (‘Founder Takes All’ or ‘density-blocking’ processes). A direct test of such processes can only, however, be carried out in real time, as populations expand into new space. Recent tectonic uplift in New Zealand and Chile eliminated intertidal biota along vast stretches of rocky shore, and the new intertidal zones are now being recolonised. These ongoing biological colonisation events present ideal opportunities to detect genetic signatures of lineage turnover. Using multi-species genomic analyses of recolonising intertidal kelp and invertebrate taxa that differ in a variety of ecological traits, our newly-funded (Marsden) study will, over the next few years, take advantage of these tectonically-disturbed systems to provide the first large-scale tests of density-blocking dynamics in real time. This poster summarises the key goals of the project, and is complemented by student presentations (Johnette Peters and Elahe Parvizi) revealing early results.
7728: Benthic communities play a major role in organic matter remineralisation and the mediation of shelf sea biogeochemistry. Few studies have considered how changes in community structure associated with different levels of physical disturbance affect sediment macronutrients and carbon content following the cessation of disturbance. Additionally, studies of the synergistic effects of ocean acidification and temperature increase rarely include the additional effect of physical disturbance as a stressor. These combined stressors have the potential to result in physical, chemical, and biological changes to this important environment with consequences for carbon sequestration, benthic food webs and biogeochemical cycling. We investigate how faunal activity (bioturbation and bioirrigation) in communities that have survived contrasting levels of bottom fishing affects benthic biogeochemistry under a future climate change scenario. We find the way communities are restructured by climate change differs with fishing frequency, with consequences for benthic nutrient remineralisation, but that changes in community structure do little to affect measured bioturbation. Our results suggest that the presence of physical disturbance and the resulting mediation of macronutrient and carbon cycling reflects the decoupling of organism-sediment relations. Disproportionate expression of specific traits post-disturbance in sediment communities exposed to different climate conditions are most important for sustaining ecosystem function.
Our changing Oceans: species and ecosystems response

7729: The carbonate equilibrium plays a crucial role in oceanic ecosystems. However, the carbonate ion is usually determined using techniques which are time-consuming and labour intensive. Given carbonate’s important role, researchers in environmental monitoring have shown growing interest in developing instrumentation capable of direct evaluation of carbonate concentration in aquatic samples. To date, limited success has been achieved with the development of carbonate Ion Selective Electrodes (ISEs), however membrane instability and insufficiently low detection limits inhibit their applicability for extended use in marine environments. Here we present an approach for determination of marine carbonate ion concentration based on simple and low-cost carbonate ISEs. An array of solid contact electrodes, which acts as the foundation for both carbonate and reference electrodes, is first created using pencil graphite applied to the surface of an acetate sheet. Initial results indicate the electrodes exhibit excellent sensing properties, including selectivity towards carbonate ions, a wide dynamic response range, fast response time, and satisfactory long-term stability. The long-term goal of this project is to deploy a 2-dimensional ISE array in a tidal rockpool, giving a real-time spatial profile and demonstrating the potential of this low-cost sensing system for monitoring carbon cycle parameters.

7730: Despite the high frequency of long-finned pilot whale (LFPW; Globicephala melas edwardii) strandings on the New Zealand coast, their diet remains poorly understood. To assess LFPW diet within New Zealand, we (1) examined stomach contents from a mass-stranding event on Farewell Spit in February 2014 (n=39), and (2) compared these to previously reported data from mass stranding events that occurred in the same location in 2005 (n=10) and 2008 (n=11). Multivariate analyses were applied to determine temporal and sex differences of hard part remains recovered in stomach contents. Prey remains were evident in 87% (n=34) of individuals from the 2014 stranding event (20 females and 14 males). Five individuals (1 female and 4 males) were recorded with empty stomachs. Prey primarily comprised cephalopod remains (542 lower and 476 upper beaks), with the lower beaks belonging exclusively to arrow squid Nototodarus spp. Fish remains were reported in the stomachs of three males – representing the first report of fish in the stomachs of LFPWs from New Zealand waters. A significantly higher number of Nototodarus beaks were recorded in the stomachs of stranded females compared to males across all years. Findings are discussed in the context of international studies of LFPW diet.
Massey University; Auckland University of Technology
7731: Heavy metals in the marine environment are concerning due to their toxicity, non-biodegradability and ability to accumulate and magnify in organisms. Biological indicator/ monitor species are a means of assessing the environment and its response to pollutants. Amphipods have been increasingly used as bioindicators of disturbed environments. Eusiroides monoculoides was collected from three sites in the Wellington region to investigate variation of trace elements across sites. There were differences among sites despite the close proximity of the study sites. Evans Bay generally had the highest concentration of trace elements. Three amphipod species when they occurred at the same site were compared. Sunamphitoe mixtura was the species with the highest concentration of trace elements. A laboratory experiment was run using sand hopper, Bellorchestia quoyana to examine whether uptake of two metals, Cu and Nd, are mediated by the presence of the other metal or an elevated seawater temperature. Amphipods from treatments with added metals had significantly higher concentrations of these metals from the controls. Temperature had no effect, and there was no interaction between the metals. Similar to S. mixtura from the field study, dry weight of B. quoyana, was negatively related to the concentration of trace elements in the body.
7732: The marine environment is of huge cultural, recreational, economic, environmental and intrinsic importance to Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ). Abundant natural ecosystems support our communities, provide for our families, and enrich our livelihoods. Human values are our guiding principles—our broadest motivations—based on what we consider to be important in life. Extensive psychological research and cross-cultural studies have identified values that occur consistently across all human beings. These values correlate strongly with people’s perceptions, attitudes and behaviours. The New Zealand Marine Values Survey (NZMVS) will measure New Zealanders’ values and their perceptions, attitudes and behaviours towards fisheries management and the marine environment. Data will be collected via an online questionnaire during August 2019 (please register at www.nzmvs.nz). Results should enable the development of new, and enhancement of existing, initiatives that seek to improve the kaitiaki of NZ’s marine environment. Dysfunctional relationships between stakeholders currently hinder progress towards outcomes that would improve the lives of all New Zealanders. The NZMVS aims to provide the impetus for values-based communication strategies and values-informed policy implementation strategies (i.e. paths of least resistance)—strategies sensitive to the diversity of values held by all New Zealanders, aimed at achieving agreement and ongoing cooperation between stakeholders.
7733: The introduction of an invasive species into a new habitat often occurs unpredictably. These introductions can cause disruption to the ecosystems and the functions that occur within. Undaria pinnatifida (Undaria) is an invasive seaweed known for its impact and worldwide presence. Since Undaria pinnatifida’s introduction to New Zealand, it has become ubiquitous in New Zealand’s shallow rocky reef ecosystems. There is a fear that Undaria is disrupting ecosystem processes due to the different traits this annual species holds compared to perennial more morphology complex native macroalgae. In the south Undaria is distributed from the intertidal to relatively low light areas in the deep subtidal (>20m). It is hypothesised that Undaria first invades in the intertidal, primarily due to thalli washing up on rocky shores and releasing their spores. The data to support this method of establishment is lacking. This study investigated which depths Undaria has become established in its recent invasion at Port Adventure, Stewart Island. This research showed that Undaria well established all around Abrahams Bosom, on the edge of spreading into Port Adventure with the highest density of establishment around 2m deep.
7734: The spinetail devilray (Mobula japanica) is caught incidentally by tuna purse seine vessels operating around northern North Island, New Zealand during summer. The species was protected in New Zealand in 2010 and efforts have since been made to develop improved handling and release methods and to estimate mortality of released rays using satellite tags. Rays are caught mainly along the north-east coast of the North Island between Great Barrier Island and the Bay of Islands. Catch rates peak along the edge of the continental shelf over seabed depths of 150-350 m. Use of a large-mesh cargo net has been promoted to ‘sieve’ the rays from the tuna as it is brailed onboard, and release the former over the side. A Code of Conduct has been developed in collaboration with the Industry. A total of 16 rays have been tagged so far, with most assessed as healthy on release, but mixed survival results recorded. The links between capture and handling conditions and survival will be discussed.
7735: Octocorals are ecologically important habitat providers for a myriad of other organisms from the intertidal to the deep sea. Many are extremely vulnerable to anthropogenic stressors, yet we remain inadequately equipped to ensure their persistence. Globally, the poor state of species-level taxonomy among octocorals has been identified as a key hurdle to their management, since clearly defined species are essential to accurately assess abundance and distribution, and formulate effective conservation strategies. While New Zealand’s EEZ hosts one of the most diverse octocoral assemblages in the world, the vast majority of our species remain undescribed. In light of this, “deadman’s fingers” (Alcyonium aurantiacum Quoy & Gaimard, 1834), a coastal, highly variable, endemic soft coral that has long been suspected of representing a species complex, was selected for taxonomic re-evaluation. Phylogenetic analyses based on mitochondrial MutS and nuclear 28S genes, complemented by microscopic examinations of sclerite morphology, confirm the presence of several, undescribed endemic species, and suggest that the erection of a new, possibly endemic genus may be warranted to accommodate them. The descriptions of these new species will contribute not only to our understanding of New Zealand’s octocoral fauna, but also to the ongoing global revision of this group’s systematics.
7736: Litter is a major risk to New Zealand’s people, culture, environment and economy, especially when it enters the marine environment. Working in collaboration with the Ministry for the Environment, Statistics New Zealand and the Department of Conservation, Sustainable Coastlines is designing and building a national litter database that portrays an accurate picture of our beach litter problem. To collect the data long-term, we have engaged with communities around Aotearoa, providing them with the training and tools required to take part in the project as ‘Citizen Scientists’, measuring beach litter flux and developing and monitoring the effectiveness of their local solutions to the growing global problem of marine litter. The data collection methodology uses a localised adaptation of the UNEP / IOC marine litter survey guidelines, co-developed by the collaborating government departments, who also worked together in the project design phase. Stats New Zealand has applied the Principles and Protocols for producers of Tier 1 Statistics to the data framework to ensure data is of a standard for use in Environment reporting. Thus, the citizen science-collected data can now be utilised for reporting on litter by government bodies nationwide, as well as for international reporting, including on the Sustainable Development Goals.
7737: Anthropogenic mortality of sharks has been a growing concern. This mortality, particularly the targeted removal of larger individuals, can result in a shift in the average size of the individuals within a population. Size is associated with many life history traits, including the relationship with age and growth rate, outlined by the Von Bertalanffy growth curve. Fecundity has also been found to be positively correlated with the size of the mother in large sharks. It was hypothesized that the size of individual sharks within a species, measured by the average length, has decreased over time. Given established correlations between body size and other life history traits, it was also hypothesized that these life history traits have changed over time. A database was built for each species of interest (Sphyrna lewini, Prionace glauca, Galeocerco cuvier, Carcharodon carcharias) from studies over past decades, evaluating changes in size and any changes in life history traits. It was found that changes varied between species. The white shark had evidence of change over time, with increasing growth rate and decreasing maximum size, which supported the hypothesis. Other species, including the blue shark, had no significant evidence of change in size or growth rate over time.
Our changing Oceans: species and ecosystems response
7738: The striped lamprey (Geotria australis) is a widely distributed (Southern Hemisphere) and culturally significant jawless fish in the family Geotriidae. Also known as kanakana (te reo) and filoko (mapudungun), the treasured species is the focus of important hereditary fisheries for both Māori and Mapuche peoples. Despite their cultural significance, much remains unknown about the biology, taxonomy, and genetics of this unique species. To reduce these uncertainties, we are completing the first comprehensive population genomics analysis of Geotria 1. in the Southern Hemisphere and 2. within New Zealand using both targeted genetic markers (Cytb) and genotyping-by sequencing (GBS) methods. Preliminary analyses of New Zealand and Argentinian striped lamprey using GBS approaches suggest these are not a panmictic population. Further Cytb and GBS comparisons of 30 individuals from nine localities in New Zealand (North: Mokau, Piha, Kaniwhaniwha, Pauatahanui, and Mangakino. South: Styx, Waiau, Waikawa, and Pourakino) revealed no genetic structure. Additional analyses including individuals from Australia, Chile, Falkland Islands, and South Georgia, should further elucidate population structure in this apparently broadly distributed species. Understanding lamprey population connectivity is critical at this time, as Geotria numbers are decreasing and lamprey populations are threatened by habitat alterations, disease, and other unidentified factors.
National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research
7739: There have been limited studies on the behaviour of the common spotty, Notolabrus celidotus, particularly regarding their ability to change sex from female to male. N. celidotus are endemic wrasse that are found ubiquitously around the NZ coastline. These polygamous fish have a hierarchical social structure with males defending breeding territories. Removal of a male from a captive breeding group will induce sex change in at least one female. It is likely that social stimuli influence the initiation of this sex change. We have developed an ethogram to categorise the range of behaviours displayed by this species to further elucidate this phenomenon. To achieve this, twenty five wild caught N. celidotus were placed in a recirculating seawater system and behaviours were recorded using underwater cameras. A total of 20 hours of footage were reviewed to develop the ethogram. The fish exhibited forty seven individual behaviours which were grouped within seven categories. In particular, we have identified twelve potential social behaviours that may influence sex change. Ultimately this ethogram will help inform further studies on sex change in N. celidotus, as well as provide essential baseline behavioural knowledge to help guide future research in this understudied species.
Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology; University of Waikato
7740: The combined effects of ocean warming and microplastics on the physiological performance of the chilean bivalve Choromytilus chorus were investigated. C. chorus individuals were exposed to four levels of microplastics (0, 2, 20, and 200 mg/l) and three of temperature (12, 15, and 18ºC) in an orthogonal combination in a twelve-week laboratory experiment. After six and twelve weeks, the physiological performance of the individuals was measured as byssus production and clearance rate; after twelve-weeks, dry soft tissue weight was measured. Generalized Linear Models (GLM) and the analysis of effect sizes showed that most of the effects were antagonistic and the magnitude of the interactive effect was similar to the main effect of temperature. In addition, only byssus production exhibited a synergistic interactive response to microplastics and warming, which was observed at the end of the experiment. Furthermore, the microplastics treatments exerted the most pronounced effect, which was limited to a significant increase in the byssus production of the individuals exposed to 20mg/l and 12ºC for 6 weeks. These results suggest that ocean warming is a key mediator of physiological responses to other stressors, microplastics in this case, and that exposure to microplastics may produce significant responses in C. chorus.
